B. Adjusting the reported value of assets to reflect their fair market value or true economic worth
C. Adjusting assets only when they are sold to recognize the gain or loss on disposal
D. Adjusting assets for inflation to maintain purchasing power of the business
questionBank.exp: The manual defines Asset Value Adjustment as: 'a financial concept used to adjust the reported value of assets on a company's balance sheet to reflect their fair market value or their true economic worth.'

questionBank.q: In the context of adjusting entries, what is the difference between an accrual and a deferral?
opts: A. An accrual occurs before cash changes hands, while a deferral occurs after cash changes hands
B. An accrual occurs after cash changes hands, while a deferral occurs before cash changes hands
C. Accruals are related only to expenses, while deferrals are related only to revenues
D. Accruals are recorded monthly, while deferrals are recorded only annually
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'An accrual occurs before a payment or receipt. A deferral occurs after a payment or receipt.' Accruals involve earning or incurring before cash exchange; deferrals involve cash exchange before earning or incurring.

questionBank.q: A company has a N30,000 balance in Accounts Receivable and a N1,500 credit balance in Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. If the company estimates that 6% of receivables will be uncollectible, what adjusting entry is needed?
opts: A. Debit Bad Debt Expense N300 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N300
B. Debit Bad Debt Expense N1,800 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N1,800
C. Debit Bad Debt Expense N300 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N1,500
D. Debit Bad Debt Expense N1,800 and Credit Accounts Receivable N1,800
questionBank.exp: Required allowance = N30,000 × 6% = N1,800. Existing allowance = N1,500 (credit). Adjustment needed = N1,800 - N1,500 = N300.

questionBank.q: Which of the following adjusting entries involves increasing both an expense and a liability?
opts: A. Recording accrued revenue for services performed but not yet billed
B. Recording accrued salaries for wages earned but not yet paid
C. Recording depreciation expense for equipment used during the period
D. Recording the expiration of prepaid insurance during the period
questionBank.exp: Accrued salaries increase the salaries expense and increase salaries payable (a liability). The manual states: 'Adjusting Entry: Increase Liability and Expense.'

questionBank.q: A company's fiscal year ends on December 31. It pays N48,000 for a 24-month insurance policy on June 1, 2023. What is the insurance expense for 2023?
opts: A. N14,000 which represents seven months of coverage used
B. N24,000 which represents twelve months of coverage used
C. N48,000 which represents the full policy cost for two years
D. N16,000 which represents eight months of coverage used
questionBank.exp: From June 1 to December 31 is 7 months. N48,000 ÷ 24 = N2,000 per month. 7 months × N2,000 = N14,000.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the allowance for doubtful accounts in financial reporting?
opts: A. To increase the reported accounts receivable balance for future sales
B. To provide for estimated losses from customers who may not pay their accounts
C. To record actual losses from customers who have declared bankruptcy
D. To set aside cash for future write-offs of uncollectible accounts
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'An Allowance for Doubtful Accounts represents a company's estimate of the accounts receivable that will not be paid, based on past experiences, industry standards, and an analysis of current economic conditions.'

questionBank.q: Under the accrual basis of accounting, when should a company record revenue from a sale of goods?
opts: A. When the goods are manufactured and ready for sale
B. When the goods are delivered and the risks and rewards transfer to the buyer
C. When the customer places an order for the goods
D. When the company receives the cash from the customer
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'revenue is recognized when goods are delivered or when services are performed... when the earning process is substantially complete - normally when the risks and rewards of ownership have passed to the buyer.'

questionBank.q: A company's adjusted trial balance shows a credit balance in Unearned Revenue of N5,000. What does this balance represent?
opts: A. Revenue that has been earned but not yet received in cash
B. An obligation to provide goods or services in the future
C. Revenue that has been earned and received in cash
D. An asset representing future cash receipts from customers
questionBank.exp: Unearned Revenue is a liability representing the obligation to provide goods or services in the future. The manual states: 'Unearned Revenue - these are previously recorded revenue that need to be adjusted... recorded in a liability account.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a deferred revenue?
opts: A. Revenue earned from services provided but not yet billed to the customer
B. Cash received from a customer for services to be performed in a future period
C. Revenue earned and received in cash during the current period
D. Revenue that is expected to be earned from future sales to customers
questionBank.exp: Deferred revenue (unearned revenue) occurs when cash is received before the revenue is earned. The manual states: 'Cash has been exchanged but the revenues are not yet earned.'

questionBank.q: What is the correct adjusting entry when a company recognizes that some of its prepaid insurance has expired during the period?
opts: A. Debit Prepaid Insurance and Credit Insurance Expense for the amount expired
B. Debit Insurance Expense and Credit Prepaid Insurance for the amount expired
C. Debit Cash and Credit Prepaid Insurance for the amount expired
D. Debit Insurance Expense and Credit Cash for the amount expired
questionBank.exp: The manual states for prepaid expenses: 'Debit Expense account for the amount used up, Credit Prepaid Expense Account.' This recognizes the expense and reduces the asset.

questionBank.q: A company's accountant recorded an adjusting entry for accrued interest income. What is the effect on the financial statements?
opts: A. Assets increase and equity increases for the amount of interest earned
B. Assets decrease and liabilities decrease for the amount of interest earned
C. Liabilities increase and equity increases for the amount of interest earned
D. Assets increase and liabilities increase for the amount of interest earned
questionBank.exp: Accrued interest income increases an asset (Interest Receivable) and increases revenue, which increases equity. The manual states: 'Adjusting Entry: Increase Asset and Revenue.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following adjusting entries involves increasing an asset and increasing a revenue?
opts: A. Recording accrued interest income on investments
B. Recording accrued salaries for wages earned but not yet paid
C. Recording the expiration of prepaid insurance
D. Recording the earning of previously deferred revenue
questionBank.exp: Accrued interest income increases interest receivable (asset) and interest income (revenue). The manual states: 'Adjusting Entry: Increase Asset and Revenue.'

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a company that has provided services to a customer but has not yet billed the customer by the end of the accounting period?
opts: A. No entry is required until the customer is billed
B. Debit Accounts Receivable and Credit Service Revenue for the unbilled amount
C. Debit Service Revenue and Credit Accounts Receivable for the unbilled amount
D. Debit Cash and Credit Service Revenue when the payment is received
questionBank.exp: This is an accrued revenue. The manual states: 'Debit Accrued Income Account - Receivables (Asset), Credit Income Account (Revenue).'

questionBank.q: A company's prepaid insurance balance decreased from N12,000 at the beginning of the year to N8,000 at the end of the year. What is the insurance expense for the year?
opts: A. N4,000 which is the decrease in the prepaid insurance balance
B. N8,000 which is the ending prepaid insurance balance
C. N12,000 which is the beginning prepaid insurance balance
D. N20,000 which is the sum of beginning and ending balances
questionBank.exp: The decrease in prepaid insurance (N12,000 - N8,000 = N4,000) represents the insurance coverage that has been used and should be recognized as expense.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of making adjusting entries for depreciation?
opts: A. To reduce the recorded cost of the asset to its market value
B. To allocate the cost of the asset over its useful life in a systematic manner
C. To provide cash for the eventual replacement of the asset
D. To reduce the asset's value for tax purposes only
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Depreciation is an accounting concept used to systematically allocate the cost of tangible assets over their useful lives.' The primary purpose is matching.

questionBank.q: Which of the following accounts would be closed to the Income Summary account at the end of the period?
opts: A. Cash which represents the company's cash on hand
B. Accounts Receivable which represents amounts owed by customers
C. Sales Revenue which represents income earned during the period
D. Accumulated Depreciation which represents depreciation taken
questionBank.exp: Sales Revenue is a temporary account (nominal account) that is closed at the end of the period. The manual states: 'Close revenue accounts to income summary.'

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of closing entries in the accounting cycle?
opts: A. To transfer balances from temporary accounts to permanent accounts
B. To record all adjusting entries for the accounting period
C. To prepare the financial statements from the trial balance
D. To verify that the trial balance is in balance
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'A closing entry is a journal entry that is made at the end of an accounting period to transfer balances from a temporary account to a permanent account.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a temporary account that is closed at the end of the period?
opts: A. Sales Revenue which represents income earned during the period
B. Rent Expense which represents costs incurred during the period
C. Dividends which represent distributions to shareholders
D. Accounts Payable which represents amounts owed to suppliers
questionBank.exp: Accounts Payable is a permanent (real) account that is carried forward to the next period. Temporary accounts include revenues, expenses, and dividends.

questionBank.q: After closing entries are made, the Income Summary account has a credit balance of N15,000. What does this indicate?
opts: A. The company had a net loss of N15,000 for the period
B. The company had net income of N15,000 for the period
C. The company made N15,000 in sales revenue
D. The company had N15,000 in expenses
questionBank.exp: A credit balance in Income Summary indicates that total revenues exceeded total expenses, resulting in net income. The balance is then closed to Retained Earnings.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct closing entry for revenue accounts?
opts: A. Debit Income Summary and Credit Revenue accounts to close revenues
B. Debit Revenue accounts and Credit Income Summary to close revenues
C. Debit Income Summary and Credit Retained Earnings to close net income
D. Debit Retained Earnings and Credit Revenue accounts to close revenues
questionBank.exp: To close revenue accounts, debit each revenue account (to zero it out) and credit Income Summary. The manual states: 'Close revenue accounts to income summary.'

questionBank.q: What is the post-closing trial balance?
opts: A. A list of all accounts after closing entries have been made, including only permanent accounts
B. A list of all accounts before closing entries have been made
C. A list of only the temporary accounts that were closed during the period
D. A list of all accounts with non-zero balances after adjusting entries
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'A post-closing trial balance is a list of balance sheet accounts with non-zero balances at the end of the reporting period. Permanent Accounts Only.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct closing entry for expense accounts?
opts: A. Debit Expense accounts and Credit Income Summary to close expenses
B. Debit Income Summary and Credit Expense accounts to close expenses
C. Debit Income Summary and Credit Retained Earnings to close expenses
D. Debit Retained Earnings and Credit Expense accounts to close expenses
questionBank.exp: To close expense accounts, debit Income Summary and credit each expense account (to zero it out). The manual states: 'Close expense accounts to income summary.'

questionBank.q: A company's trial balance shows Salaries Expense of N45,000. What is the closing entry for this account?
opts: A. Debit Salaries Expense N45,000 and Credit Income Summary N45,000 to close the expense
B. Debit Income Summary N45,000 and Credit Salaries Expense N45,000 to close the expense
C. Debit Salaries Expense N45,000 and Credit Retained Earnings N45,000 to close the expense
D. Debit Cash N45,000 and Credit Salaries Expense N45,000 to reverse the expense
questionBank.exp: To close expense accounts, debit Income Summary and credit the expense accounts. This transfers the expense balance to Income Summary.

questionBank.q: What is the effect on the accounting equation when closing entries are made?
opts: A. Total assets and total liabilities change significantly
B. Retained earnings is updated, and total assets remain unchanged
C. Revenue and expense accounts are reduced to zero balances
D. Both assets and liabilities are reset to their beginning balances
questionBank.exp: Closing entries reset temporary accounts to zero and update retained earnings. Total assets and liabilities remain unchanged by closing entries, as the entries only transfer balances between equity accounts.

questionBank.q: After closing entries are made, the Income Summary account has a debit balance of N8,000. What does this indicate?
opts: A. The company had net income of N8,000 for the period
B. The company had a net loss of N8,000 for the period
C. The company made N8,000 in sales revenue
D. The company had N8,000 in total expenses
questionBank.exp: A debit balance in Income Summary indicates that total expenses exceeded total revenues, resulting in a net loss. The balance is then closed to Retained Earnings.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct closing entry for the Income Summary account when the company has net income?
opts: A. Debit Retained Earnings and Credit Income Summary for the net income amount
B. Debit Income Summary and Credit Retained Earnings for the net income amount
C. Debit Income Summary and Credit Capital for the net income amount
D. Debit Cash and Credit Income Summary for the net income amount
questionBank.exp: When there is net income, the Income Summary account has a credit balance. To close it, debit Income Summary and credit Retained Earnings. The manual states: 'Close income summary to retained earnings.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following accounts would appear on the post-closing trial balance?
opts: A. Sales Revenue because it is a revenue account with a balance
B. Rent Expense because it is an expense account with a balance
C. Cash because it is an asset account with a balance
D. Dividends because they are distributed to shareholders
questionBank.exp: The post-closing trial balance includes only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, equity). Cash is a permanent account that remains on the books.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the Income Summary account?
opts: A. To serve as a temporary account to summarize revenues and expenses before closing to retained earnings
B. To provide a summary of all income and expenses for management reporting purposes
C. To record all revenue transactions during the accounting period
D. To replace the need for the Statement of Profit or Loss
questionBank.exp: The Income Summary account is a temporary clearing account used to close revenue and expense accounts. It summarizes the period's revenues and expenses to determine net income or loss.

questionBank.q: A company's post-closing trial balance shows a credit balance of N100,000 in Retained Earnings. What does this balance represent?
opts: A. The total dividends paid to shareholders during the period
B. The beginning retained earnings balance plus net income less dividends
C. The total revenue earned by the company during the period
D. The total assets of the company less total liabilities
questionBank.exp: Retained Earnings is the cumulative net income (or loss) less dividends since the company's inception. The post-closing balance includes the updated balance after closing entries.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct closing entry for Dividends?
opts: A. Debit Retained Earnings and Credit Dividends to close the dividend account
B. Debit Dividends and Credit Retained Earnings to close the dividend account
C. Debit Income Summary and Credit Dividends to close the dividend account
D. Debit Dividends and Credit Income Summary to close the dividend account
questionBank.exp: Dividends are closed to Retained Earnings by debiting Retained Earnings and crediting Dividends. The manual states: 'Close dividends (or withdrawals) to retained earnings.'

questionBank.q: What is the primary difference between the adjusted trial balance and the post-closing trial balance?
opts: A. The adjusted trial balance includes only permanent accounts, while the post-closing includes all accounts
B. The post-closing trial balance includes only permanent accounts, while the adjusted includes all accounts
C. The adjusted trial balance is prepared before adjustments, while the post-closing is prepared after
D. There is no difference between the adjusted and post-closing trial balances
questionBank.exp: The adjusted trial balance includes all accounts after adjustments. The post-closing trial balance includes only permanent accounts after closing entries have been made.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly describes the closing process for a company that has a net loss?
opts: A. Close revenues and expenses to Income Summary, then close Income Summary (debit) to Retained Earnings (credit)
B. Close revenues and expenses to Income Summary, then close Income Summary (credit) to Retained Earnings (debit)
C. Close only revenues to Income Summary, then close Income Summary to Retained Earnings
D. Close only expenses to Income Summary, then close Income Summary to Retained Earnings
questionBank.exp: When there is a net loss, Income Summary has a debit balance. Closing Income Summary requires crediting Income Summary and debiting Retained Earnings. The process is the same, just the direction differs.

questionBank.q: Why are temporary accounts closed at the end of each accounting period?
opts: A. To reduce the number of accounts in the general ledger for the next period
B. To allow the company to compare income and expenses across different periods
C. To prepare the accounts for the preparation of the Statement of Financial Position
D. To ensure that tax calculations are based on the correct accounting period
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Having a zero balance in these accounts is important so a business can compare performance across periods, particularly with income.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the closing process?
opts: A. Close revenue accounts to the Income Summary account
B. Close expense accounts to the Income Summary account
C. Close Income Summary to the Retained Earnings account
D. Close asset accounts to the Retained Earnings account
questionBank.exp: Asset accounts are permanent accounts and are never closed. Only temporary accounts (revenues, expenses, dividends) are closed to retained earnings.

questionBank.q: A company has total revenues of N250,000 and total expenses of N230,000. What is the closing entry for Income Summary?
opts: A. Debit Income Summary N20,000 and Credit Retained Earnings N20,000 for net income
B. Debit Retained Earnings N20,000 and Credit Income Summary N20,000 for net income
C. Debit Income Summary N20,000 and Credit Cash N20,000 for net income
D. Debit Cash N20,000 and Credit Income Summary N20,000 for net income
questionBank.exp: Net income is N250,000 - N230,000 = N20,000. Income Summary has a credit balance. To close it, debit Income Summary and credit Retained Earnings.

questionBank.q: After the closing process, which accounts have zero balances?
opts: A. All asset and liability accounts
B. All revenue, expense, and dividend accounts
C. All balance sheet accounts
D. Only the Income Summary account
questionBank.exp: Revenue, expense, and dividend accounts are temporary accounts that are closed to zero at the end of each period. Assets and liabilities are permanent accounts.

questionBank.q: What is the first step in the closing process?
opts: A. Close expense accounts to Income Summary
B. Close Income Summary to Retained Earnings
C. Close revenue accounts to Income Summary
D. Close Dividends to Retained Earnings
questionBank.exp: The manual lists the steps in order: Close revenue accounts to income summary (first), Close expense accounts to income summary (second), Close income summary to retained earnings (third), and Close dividends (or withdrawals) to retained earnings (fourth).

questionBank.q: A company's post-closing trial balance includes which of the following types of accounts?
opts: A. Revenue, expense, and dividend accounts
B. Only assets and liabilities
C. Asset, liability, and equity accounts
D. Only equity accounts
questionBank.exp: The post-closing trial balance includes only permanent accounts: assets, liabilities, and equity accounts. Temporary accounts have been closed to zero.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about closing entries?
opts: A. Closing entries are made before adjusting entries in the accounting cycle
B. Closing entries are made at the beginning of the accounting period
C. Closing entries transfer balances from temporary to permanent accounts
D. Closing entries are optional for companies with small revenues
questionBank.exp: Closing entries transfer balances from temporary accounts to permanent accounts. They are made at the end of the accounting period after adjusting entries.

questionBank.q: After closing entries, a company's Dividends account has a balance of N0. What does this indicate?
opts: A. The company did not pay dividends during the period
B. The Dividends account was closed to Retained Earnings
C. The Dividends account balance was transferred to expenses
D. The Dividends account has been permanently eliminated
questionBank.exp: Dividends are a temporary account. The closing entry debits Retained Earnings and credits Dividends, resulting in a zero balance in the Dividends account.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of preparing a bank reconciliation statement?
opts: A. To identify all cash transactions that occurred during the accounting period
B. To compare the company's accounting records with the bank statement and identify differences
C. To prepare the cash flow statement for the accounting period
D. To calculate the company's net profit or loss for the period
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Bank reconciliation is a financial process that compares a company's internal financial records with the records provided by its bank or financial institution. It is used to identify and resolve discrepancies.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following would cause the company's cash book balance to differ from the bank statement balance?
opts: A. The company records all cash receipts in its books immediately
B. The bank processes all transactions on the same day they occur
C. Outstanding checks that have been issued but not yet presented to the bank
D. The bank statement is prepared on the same date as the company's year-end
questionBank.exp: Outstanding checks (unpresented cheques) are a common reason for differences. The manual states: 'Unpresented cheques - Checks that have been issued by the company to creditors but have not been presented for payment.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as an unpresented cheque?
opts: A. A cheque received from a customer that has been deposited and cleared by the bank
B. A cheque issued by the company that has not yet been presented to the bank for payment
C. A cheque received from a customer that has been deposited but not yet credited by the bank
D. A cheque that was issued by the company and presented for payment
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Unpresented cheques / Outstanding checks: Checks that have been issued by the company to creditors but have not been presented for payment or the payments have not yet been processed.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be added to the balance per bank statement when reconciling?
opts: A. Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
B. Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
C. Bank charges that were deducted by the bank
D. Dishonoured cheques returned by the bank
questionBank.exp: Uncredited cheques (deposits in transit) have been recorded by the company but not yet credited by the bank. They are added to the bank statement balance. The format shows: 'Less uncredited Cheques' when reconciling from the cash book balance.

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a credit balance of N5,000. What does this indicate?
opts: A. The company has cash in hand of N5,000
B. The company has a bank overdraft of N5,000
C. The company has cash at bank of N5,000
D. The company has received N5,000 from customers
questionBank.exp: A credit balance in the cash book indicates a bank overdraft, which is a liability. A debit balance indicates cash at bank, which is an asset.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be deducted from the balance per cash book when preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
B. Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
C. Bank charges that were deducted by the bank but not recorded in the cash book
D. Direct deposits made by customers that were credited by the bank
questionBank.exp: Bank charges are deducted by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the company's cash book. They are deducted from the cash book balance when reconciling.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be added to the balance per cash book when preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Unpresented cheques that have not yet cleared the bank
B. Uncredited cheques that have not yet been credited by the bank
C. Bank charges that were deducted by the bank
D. Direct deposits (NIBSS credits) that were credited by the bank but not recorded in the cash book
questionBank.exp: Direct deposits or NIBSS credits are credited by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the company's cash book. They are added to the cash book balance when reconciling.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a timing difference that causes the cash book and bank statement to differ?
opts: A. Bank charges that are deducted by the bank
B. The company recording an incorrect cheque amount in the cash book
C. A deposit in transit that has been recorded by the company but not by the bank
D. A dishonoured cheque that was returned by the bank
questionBank.exp: A deposit in transit is a timing difference because the company has recorded the deposit, but the bank has not yet processed and recorded it. The manual identifies uncredited cheques as a timing difference.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a dishonoured cheque in the bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Add it to the cash book balance because the bank has processed it
B. Deduct it from the cash book balance because the amount was not received
C. Add it to the bank statement balance because it represents a customer payment
D. Ignore it because it will be processed in the next period
questionBank.exp: A dishonoured cheque (bounced cheque) was previously recorded as a receipt in the cash book. When the bank returns it, the cash book must be adjusted by deducting the amount.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of preparing an adjusted cash book as part of the bank reconciliation process?
opts: A. To record all transactions that appear in the cash book but not in the bank statement
B. To update the cash book for transactions that appear in the bank statement but not in the cash book
C. To calculate the net profit or loss for the accounting period
D. To prepare the bank reconciliation statement directly
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Prepare the adjusted cash book by debiting it with all legitimate items credited in the bank statement and credit the cash book with all legitimate items debited in the bank statement.'

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a balance of N10,000. Bank charges of N500 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: A. N10,500 which is the cash book balance plus the bank charges
B. N9,500 which is the cash book balance less the bank charges
C. N10,000 which is the cash book balance unchanged
D. N9,500 which is the cash book balance less the bank charges
questionBank.exp: Bank charges are expenses that reduce the cash balance. They must be deducted from the cash book: N10,000 - N500 = N9,500.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for difference between the bank statement and the company's accounting records?
opts: A. Unpresented cheques that have been issued but not yet presented
B. Uncredited cheques that have been deposited but not yet credited
C. The company's accounting records are based on accrual accounting
D. Bank charges that have been deducted by the bank
questionBank.exp: Accrual accounting is a basis of accounting, not a reason for difference between the bank statement and cash book. The differences are caused by timing differences and items recorded by one party but not the other.

questionBank.q: A company's bank statement shows a credit balance of N25,000. The company has unpresented cheques of N3,000 and uncredited cheques of N5,000. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: A. N23,000 which is the bank balance adjusted for unpresented and uncredited cheques
B. N27,000 which is the bank balance plus unpresented less uncredited
C. N25,000 which is the bank balance unchanged by these items
D. N30,000 which is the bank balance plus uncredited cheques
questionBank.exp: Adjusted Cash Book = Bank Statement - Unpresented + Uncredited = N25,000 - N3,000 + N5,000 = N27,000.

questionBank.q: What is a standing order in the context of bank reconciliation?
opts: A. A cheque that has been issued but not yet presented to the bank
B. A regular automatic payment set up by the account holder to pay a fixed amount
C. A deposit made by the company that has not yet been credited by the bank
D. A direct credit made by the bank to the company's account
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'A standing order is a financial arrangement that allows an account holder to set up automatic, recurring payments to be made from their bank account to another account on a fixed schedule.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a direct debit in the bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Add it to the cash book balance because the bank has debited the account
B. Deduct it from the cash book balance because the bank has made a payment on behalf of the company
C. Add it to the bank statement balance because it represents a bank charge
D. Ignore it until the company receives notification from the bank
questionBank.exp: A direct debit is a payment made automatically from the company's bank account. The bank records it on the bank statement, but it may not yet be recorded in the cash book. It should be deducted from the cash book balance.

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a debit balance of N15,000. The bank statement shows a credit balance of N18,000. Which of the following is a possible explanation for the difference?
opts: A. The company has unpresented cheques of N3,000 that have not yet been cleared
B. The company has uncredited cheques of N3,000 that have not yet been credited by the bank
C. The bank has deducted N3,000 in charges that were not recorded in the cash book
D. The company has not recorded a N3,000 direct deposit from a customer
questionBank.exp: If the cash book balance is lower than the bank statement balance (N15,000 vs N18,000), the company must have issued cheques that haven't been presented (unpresented cheques). These reduce the cash book balance but the bank doesn't know about them yet.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would NOT appear on a bank reconciliation statement?
opts: A. Unpresented cheques that have been issued but not yet presented
B. Uncredited cheques that have been deposited but not yet credited
C. Bank charges that have been deducted but not yet recorded in the cash book
D. Depreciation expense for the accounting period
questionBank.exp: Depreciation expense is a non-cash item that does not affect the bank account. It would not appear on a bank reconciliation statement, which only deals with cash and bank transactions.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a cheque issued to a supplier that remains unpresented at the end of the accounting period?
opts: A. Deduct it from the bank statement balance in the reconciliation statement
B. Add it to the bank statement balance in the reconciliation statement
C. Deduct it from the cash book balance in the reconciliation statement
D. No adjustment is required because it is a timing difference
questionBank.exp: Unpresented cheques have been recorded in the cash book (reducing the balance) but not yet processed by the bank. When reconciling from the bank statement balance, unpresented cheques are deducted.

questionBank.q: A company's bank reconciliation shows a difference of N2,000. After investigation, it is found that the bank had incorrectly debited the company's account. What is the correct treatment?
opts: A. Adjust the cash book balance by adding N2,000
B. Adjust the cash book balance by deducting N2,000
C. Contact the bank to correct the error and not adjust the cash book
D. Adjust the bank statement balance by adding N2,000
questionBank.exp: If the bank has made an error, the correction should be made by the bank. The company should contact the bank to correct the error rather than adjusting the cash book. However, in the reconciliation, the error would appear as an 'other error' in the bank.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct format for a bank reconciliation statement when starting from the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: A. Adjusted Cash Book Balance + Unpresented Cheques - Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
B. Adjusted Cash Book Balance - Unpresented Cheques + Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
C. Adjusted Cash Book Balance + Unpresented Cheques + Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
D. Adjusted Cash Book Balance - Unpresented Cheques - Uncredited Cheques = Bank Statement Balance
questionBank.exp: The manual shows the format: 'Balance as per adjusted Cash Book + Add Unpresented Cheques - Less uncredited Cheques = Balance as per Bank Statement.'

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a balance of N20,000. The bank statement shows a balance of N18,000. The difference is a N2,000 cheque issued to a supplier that has not yet been presented. What is the correct reconciliation?
opts: A. Cash Book N20,000 - Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Bank Statement N18,000
B. Cash Book N20,000 + Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Bank Statement N22,000
C. Bank Statement N18,000 + Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Cash Book N20,000
D. Bank Statement N18,000 - Unpresented Cheque N2,000 = Cash Book N16,000
questionBank.exp: The company has recorded the payment in the cash book (N20,000), but the bank hasn't processed it yet, so the bank balance is higher (N18,000). The unpresented cheque of N2,000 is deducted from the cash book balance to arrive at the bank statement balance: N20,000 - N2,000 = N18,000.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a reason for preparing bank reconciliation statements regularly?
opts: A. To identify cash transactions that have been recorded in error
B. To ensure all deposits and withdrawals are accurately recorded
C. To detect fraud and unauthorized transactions
D. All of the above
questionBank.exp: The manual states the importance of bank reconciliation includes: 'Accuracy Assurance: ensures company's cash balance matches actual bank balance,' 'Fraud Detection: can help detect unauthorized transactions,' and 'Error Identification: discrepancies may highlight errors.'

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a NIBSS credit in the bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Add it to the cash book balance because it is a direct deposit to the company's account
B. Deduct it from the cash book balance because it is a bank fee
C. Add it to the bank statement balance because it is a timing difference
D. Ignore it because it is not a cash transaction
questionBank.exp: A NIBSS credit (direct deposit) is credited by the bank but may not yet be recorded in the cash book. It should be added to the cash book balance. The manual's example shows a 'NIBSS Credit 24' in the bank statement that needs to be recorded in the cash book.

questionBank.q: A company's cash book shows a balance of N30,000. Bank charges of N400 and direct deposit of N2,000 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: A. N32,400 which is the cash book balance plus direct deposit less bank charges
B. N31,600 which is the cash book balance plus direct deposit less bank charges
C. N30,000 which is the cash book balance unchanged by these items
D. N32,400 which is the cash book balance plus bank charges less direct deposit
questionBank.exp: Adjusted cash book = N30,000 + N2,000 (direct deposit) - N400 (bank charges) = N31,600.

questionBank.q: Which of the following errors would cause the cash book balance to be overstated?
opts: A. A cheque issued to a supplier was recorded as N5,000 instead of N500 in the cash book
B. A cheque received from a customer was recorded as N500 instead of N5,000 in the cash book
C. Bank charges were recorded as income instead of expenses in the cash book
D. A direct deposit from a customer was not recorded in the cash book
questionBank.exp: If a cheque received from a customer was recorded as N5,000 instead of the actual N500, the cash book balance would be overstated by N4,500.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for a cheque that was deposited by the company but was returned by the bank as dishonoured?
opts: A. Deduct the cheque amount from the cash book balance
B. Add the cheque amount to the cash book balance
C. Deduct the cheque amount from the bank statement balance
D. Add the cheque amount to the bank statement balance
questionBank.exp: A dishonoured cheque was previously recorded as a receipt in the cash book. When the bank returns it, the cash book must be adjusted by deducting the amount. The manual identifies 'Dishonoured Cheques' as a reason for difference.

questionBank.q: A company has unpresented cheques of N8,000 and uncredited cheques of N5,000. The bank statement shows a balance of N25,000. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
opts: A. N22,000 which is the bank balance plus unpresented less uncredited
B. N20,000 which is the bank balance plus uncredited less unpresented
C. N28,000 which is the bank balance plus uncredited and unpresented
D. N30,000 which is the bank balance plus unpresented and uncredited
questionBank.exp: Adjusted Cash Book = Bank Statement - Unpresented + Uncredited = N25,000 - N8,000 + N5,000 = N22,000.

questionBank.q: What is the correct treatment for bank interest earned that appears on the bank statement but not in the cash book?
opts: A. Debit the cash book with the interest amount
B. Credit the cash book with the interest amount
C. Debit the bank statement with the interest amount
D. Credit the bank statement with the interest amount
questionBank.exp: Bank interest earned is income that increases the bank balance. It should be recorded in the cash book as a debit (increase in the asset). The manual identifies 'Interest Earnings' as a reason for difference.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence for preparing a bank reconciliation?
opts: A. Prepare bank reconciliation statement directly from cash book and bank statement
B. Prepare adjusted cash book, then bank reconciliation statement
C. Prepare bank statement first, then adjusted cash book, then reconciliation
D. Prepare adjusted cash book and bank reconciliation statement simultaneously
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'a. Prepare the adjusted cash book by debiting it with all legitimate items credited in the bank statement and credit the cash book with all legitimate items debited in the bank statement. b. Prepare the Bank Reconciliation Statement.'

questionBank.q: A company's cash book balance is N15,000. After preparing a bank reconciliation, the adjusted balance is N18,000. What does this indicate about the company's cash position?
opts: A. The company has N15,000 in cash which is the cash book balance
B. The company has N18,000 in cash which is the adjusted balance
C. The company has a bank overdraft of N15,000
D. The company has N3,000 in unpresented cheques
questionBank.exp: The adjusted cash book balance represents the true cash balance after accounting for all items that appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. This is the balance that should be reported in the financial statements.

questionBank.q: When a customer deposits N100,000 into their current account, what is the correct accounting entry for the bank?
opts: A. Debit Cash Account and Credit Customer's Current Account for the full deposit amount
B. Credit Cash Account and Debit Customer's Current Account for the full deposit amount
C. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Loan Account for the full deposit amount
D. Credit Customer's Current Account and Debit Interest Income for the full deposit amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer deposits N100,000 in a current account: Dr: Cash Account (Asset) N100,000, Cr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N100,000.' Deposits are liabilities for the bank.

questionBank.q: When a bank earns interest income of N250,000 but has not yet received the cash, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Income for the interest earned but not yet received
B. Debit Interest Receivable and Credit Interest Income for the interest earned but not yet received
C. Debit Interest Income and Credit Interest Receivable for the interest earned but not yet received
D. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Receivable for the interest earned but not yet received
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank earns Interest income of N250,000 but has not yet received the income: Dr: Interest Receivable (Asset) N250,000, Cr: Interest Income (Revenue) N250,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank originates a N1,200,000 loan to a customer, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: A. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the loan amount
B. Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account and Credit Customer's Current Account for the loan amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the loan disbursement
D. Debit Interest Income and Credit Customer's Current Account for the loan amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank originates a N1,200,000 loan... Dr: Customer's Loan Receivable Account (Asset) N1,200,000, Cr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N1,200,000.'

questionBank.q: A customer makes a loan repayment of N115,000 which includes N100,000 principal and N15,000 interest. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the full amount
B. Debit Customer's Current Account, Credit Customer's Loan Receivable N100,000, and Credit Interest Income N15,000
C. Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account and Credit Interest Income for the full amount
D. Debit Interest Income and Credit Customer's Current Account for the full repayment amount
questionBank.exp: The manual shows: 'When the customer makes a repayment of N115,000... Dr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N115,000, Cr: Customer's Loan Receivable Account (Asset) N100,000, Cr: Interest Income (Revenue) N15,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank purchases N50,000,000 in government bonds, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: A. Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the purchase amount
B. Credit Investment in Government Bonds and Debit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the purchase amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the bond purchase
D. Credit Investment in Government Bonds and Debit Interest Income for the bond purchase
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank purchases N50,000,000 worth of government bonds: Dr: Investment in Government Bonds (Asset) N50,000,000, Cr: Bank's CBN Operating Account (Asset) N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct entry when a bank records interest expense of N120,000 that has been incurred but not yet paid?
opts: A. Debit Interest Payable and Credit Interest Expense for the accrued interest
B. Debit Interest Expense and Credit Interest Payable for the accrued interest
C. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Expense for the interest incurred
D. Debit Interest Expense and Credit Cash for the interest incurred
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank incurs interest expense of N120,000 but has not yet paid: Dr: Interest Expense (Expense) N120,000, Cr: Interest Payable (Liability) N120,000.'

questionBank.q: When a customer purchases a N500,000 Certificate of Deposit, what is the correct accounting entry for the bank?
opts: A. Debit Certificate of Deposit and Credit Customer's Current Account for the CD purchase
B. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Certificate of Deposit for the CD purchase
C. Debit Certificate of Deposit and Credit Interest Income for the CD purchase
D. Debit Cash and Credit Certificate of Deposit for the CD purchase
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer purchases a N500,000 CD: Dr: Customer's Current/Savings Account (Liability) N500,000, Cr: Certificate of Deposit (Liability) N500,000.'

questionBank.q: A bank sells government bonds for N50,050,000 when the carrying amount is N50,000,000. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Credit Realized Gain N50,000
B. Credit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Debit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Debit Realized Gain N50,000
C. Debit CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,050,000, and Credit Realized Gain N50,000
D. Debit CBN Operating Account N50,000,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,050,000, and Debit Realized Loss N50,000
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sells the investments for proceeds of N50,050,000... Dr: CBN Operating Account N50,050,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, Cr: Realized Gain Account N50,000.'

questionBank.q: A bank sells government bonds for N49,975,000 when the carrying amount is N50,000,000. What is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit CBN Operating Account N50,000,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N49,975,000, and Credit Realized Gain N25,000
B. Debit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Debit Realized Loss N25,000, and Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000
C. Credit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Credit Realized Loss N25,000, and Debit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000
D. Debit CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Credit Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000, and Credit Realized Gain N25,000
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sells the investments for proceeds of N49,975,000... Dr: CBN Operating Account N49,975,000, Dr: Realized Loss N25,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank sets aside a N100,000,000 provision for loan losses, what is the correct accounting entry?
opts: A. Debit Loan Loss Reserves and Credit Loan Loss Expense for the provision amount
B. Debit Loan Loss Expense and Credit Loan Loss Reserves for the provision amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Loan Loss Reserves for the provision amount
D. Debit Loan Loss Expense and Credit Cash for the provision amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank sets aside a N100,000,000 as loan loss provision: Dr: Loan Loss Expense (Income Statement) N100,000,000, Cr: Loan Loss Reserves (Contra Asset) N100,000,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the role of accounting in ensuring regulatory compliance for banks?
opts: A. Accounting helps banks avoid paying taxes by minimizing reported income
B. Accounting enables banks to measure capital adequacy and meet Basel III reporting requirements
C. Accounting allows banks to delay the recognition of losses for regulatory purposes
D. Accounting ensures that banks can maximize their profits by choosing favorable accounting methods
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting standards are essential for meeting regulatory requirements, such as those set forth by Basel III. Banks must maintain sufficient capital reserves, and accurate accounting is crucial for measuring capital adequacy.'

questionBank.q: When a bank pays the interest expense that was previously accrued, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Interest Payable and Credit Cash for the interest payment
B. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Payable for the interest payment
C. Debit Interest Expense and Credit Interest Payable for the interest payment
D. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Expense for the interest payment
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank eventually pays the interest expense: Dr: Interest Payable (Liability) N120,000, Cr: Cash/CBN Operating Account (Asset) N120,000.'

questionBank.q: When a bank receives interest income that was previously accrued, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Interest Income and Credit Interest Receivable for the interest received
B. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Receivable for the interest received
C. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Income for the interest received
D. Debit Interest Receivable and Credit Cash for the interest received
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank eventually receives the interest income: Dr: Cash/CBN Operating Account (Asset) N250,000, Cr: Interest Receivable (Asset) N250,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct entry when a customer withdraws N50,000 by writing a cheque?
opts: A. Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Current Account for the withdrawal amount
B. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Cash for the withdrawal amount
C. Debit Customer's Loan Account and Credit Cash for the withdrawal amount
D. Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Loan Account for the withdrawal amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When a customer writes a check for N50,000: Dr: Customer's Current Account (Liability) N50,000, Cr: Cash (Asset) N50,000.'

questionBank.q: When a CD matures and the bank pays the customer N525,000 (N500,000 principal plus N25,000 interest), what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Certificate of Deposit N525,000 and Credit Cash N525,000 for the full payment
B. Debit Certificate of Deposit N500,000, Debit Interest Expense N25,000, and Credit Cash N525,000
C. Debit Cash N525,000, Credit Certificate of Deposit N500,000, and Credit Interest Income N25,000
D. Debit Interest Expense N25,000 and Credit Certificate of Deposit N500,000 for the full payment
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the CD matures and the bank pays the customer N525,000... Dr: Certificate of Deposit (Liability) N500,000, Dr: Interest Expense (Expense) N25,000, Cr: Cash/CBN Operating Account (Asset) N525,000.'

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of the Loan Loss Reserves account in banking?
opts: A. To record the actual losses from loans that have been written off as uncollectible
B. To provide a cushion for expected future loan defaults based on historical experience
C. To set aside cash for dividend payments to shareholders
D. To reduce the bank's tax liability by recognizing expenses
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Banks must set aside provisions for loan losses to account for potential defaults on loans. This is an accounting expense that reduces net income.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways accounting supports decision-making in banking?
opts: A. Performance analysis through ratios like ROA and ROE
B. Budgeting and forecasting based on historical financial records
C. Risk management through stress testing and scenario analysis
D. Determining employee salaries and compensation packages
questionBank.exp: The manual lists performance analysis, budgeting and forecasting, and risk management as ways accounting supports decision-making. Employee compensation is not identified as a primary accounting function in banking.

questionBank.q: When a bank receives N10,000 in interest income from its investments, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Interest Income and Credit Bank's CBN Operating Account for the interest received
B. Debit Bank's CBN Operating Account and Credit Interest Income for the interest received
C. Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Interest Income for the interest received
D. Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the interest received
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the bank receives N10,000 in interest income from its investments: Dr: Bank's CBN Operating Account (Asset) N10,000, Cr: Interest Income (Income Statement) N10,000.'

questionBank.q: When investments mature and the bank receives N50,000,000, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit CBN Operating Account for the maturity amount
B. Debit CBN Operating Account and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the maturity amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Investment in Government Bonds for the maturity amount
D. Debit Investment in Government Bonds and Credit Interest Income for the maturity amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When the investments mature: Dr: CBN Operating Account (Asset) N50,000,000, Cr: Investment in Government Bonds (Asset) N50,000,000.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following describes how accounting helps banks detect money laundering and fraud?
opts: A. Accounting eliminates the need for Know Your Customer procedures
B. Accounting helps banks monitor account activity and identify unusual patterns
C. Accounting allows banks to avoid reporting suspicious transactions
D. Accounting ensures that all customer transactions are approved by management
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting helps banks detect suspicious transactions and comply with AML regulations. Banks monitor account activity and use accounting data to identify unusual patterns.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct treatment for a bank's customer deposits in the context of the accounting equation?
opts: A. Deposits are assets because they represent cash held by the bank
B. Deposits are liabilities because the bank owes the deposited funds to customers
C. Deposits are equity because they represent ownership in the bank
D. Deposits are revenue because they generate fee income for the bank
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When customers deposit funds into their bank accounts... banks must record these deposits as liabilities because they owe the deposited amount to the customers.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why accurate accounting is important for tax compliance in banking?
opts: A. Banks must report income and pay taxes on interest earned
B. Banks must report income and pay taxes on dividends and capital gains
C. Banks must ensure all tax payments are made on time to avoid penalties
D. Banks must calculate depreciation on loans to reduce taxable income
questionBank.exp: Depreciation is not calculated on loans. The manual states: 'Accurate accounting is vital for tax compliance. Banks must report income and pay taxes on interest, dividends, and capital gains.'

questionBank.q: When a bank's customer makes a loan payment that includes only principal (no interest), what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Customer's Current Account and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the principal amount
B. Credit Customer's Current Account and Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account for the principal amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Interest Income for the principal amount
D. Debit Customer's Loan Receivable Account and Credit Cash for the principal amount
questionBank.exp: A principal-only payment reduces the loan receivable (asset) and reduces the customer's current account (liability). The entry is: Debit Customer's Current Account, Credit Customer's Loan Receivable Account.

questionBank.q: What is the role of accounting in asset and liability management for banks?
opts: A. To ensure that the bank can meet its obligations to depositors while generating income from assets
B. To maximize the bank's profits by investing in high-risk assets
C. To reduce the bank's liabilities by encouraging customers to withdraw deposits
D. To ensure that all bank assets are fully insured by the government
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Banks rely on accounting to manage assets and liabilities effectively. Accurate records facilitate asset and liability matching, ensuring that the bank can meet its obligations to depositors while generating income from its assets.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct entry when a bank writes off an uncollectible loan that was previously fully provided for?
opts: A. Debit Loan Loss Reserve and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable for the write-off amount
B. Debit Loan Loss Expense and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable for the write-off amount
C. Debit Cash and Credit Customer's Loan Receivable for the write-off amount
D. Debit Customer's Loan Receivable and Credit Loan Loss Reserve for the write-off amount
questionBank.exp: When a loan is written off and a provision already exists, the entry reduces the loan loss reserve (contra-asset) and reduces the loan receivable (asset).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of a bank's regulatory reporting requirements?
opts: A. Balance sheet showing assets, liabilities, and equity
B. Income statement showing revenues and expenses
C. Statement of cash flows showing cash inflows and outflows
D. Statement of employee satisfaction and human resources metrics
questionBank.exp: Regulatory reporting includes balance sheets and income statements. Employee satisfaction metrics are not part of regulatory reporting requirements.

questionBank.q: When a bank originates a loan, how is the loan classified on the bank's Statement of Financial Position?
opts: A. As a liability because the bank will receive future cash flows from the customer
B. As an asset because it represents a future economic benefit from the customer's repayments
C. As equity because the loan increases the bank's capital base
D. As revenue because the loan generates interest income for the bank
questionBank.exp: A loan receivable is an asset for the bank because it represents the right to receive future cash flows from the borrower.

questionBank.q: What is the effect on the bank's accounting equation when a customer deposits N50,000 into a savings account?
opts: A. Assets increase by N50,000 and liabilities increase by N50,000
B. Assets decrease by N50,000 and liabilities decrease by N50,000
C. Assets increase by N50,000 and equity increase by N50,000
D. Liabilities increase by N50,000 and equity decrease by N50,000
questionBank.exp: The bank receives cash (asset increases) and creates a deposit liability (liability increases). Equity remains unchanged.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between accounting and risk management in banking?
opts: A. Accounting is primarily used to hide risk from regulators and investors
B. Accounting provides data that helps banks identify, measure, and manage financial risks
C. Accounting eliminates all operational risks in banking operations
D. Accounting is only relevant for historical reporting, not future risk management
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Accounting plays a crucial role in risk assessment and management. Banks use accounting data to identify credit, liquidity, and operational risks.'

questionBank.q: When a bank pays N250,000 in salaries to its employees, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Salaries Expense and Credit Cash for the salary payment
B. Credit Salaries Expense and Debit Cash for the salary payment
C. Debit Salaries Payable and Credit Cash for the salary payment
D. Debit Cash and Credit Salaries Expense for the salary payment
questionBank.exp: Paying salaries increases the salaries expense (debit) and decreases cash (credit). This is a standard accounting entry.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of creating an allowance for doubtful accounts?
opts: A. To record actual losses from customers who have declared bankruptcy
B. To estimate the portion of accounts receivable that may not be collected
C. To increase the accounts receivable balance for future sales
D. To set aside cash for future write-offs of uncollectible accounts
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'An Allowance for Doubtful Accounts represents a company's estimate of the accounts receivable that will not be paid, based on past experiences, industry standards, and an analysis of current economic conditions.'

questionBank.q: If a company has accounts receivable of N200,000 and estimates that 4% will be uncollectible, what is the bad debt expense?
opts: A. N4,000 which is 2% of the accounts receivable balance
B. N8,000 which is 4% of the accounts receivable balance
C. N12,000 which is 6% of the accounts receivable balance
D. N16,000 which is 8% of the accounts receivable balance
questionBank.exp: Bad debt expense = Accounts Receivable × Bad Debt Percentage = N200,000 × 4% = N8,000.

questionBank.q: A company's accounts receivable aging schedule shows the following: 0-30 days: N50,000 (1% uncollectible), 31-60 days: N20,000 (5% uncollectible). What is the total estimated uncollectible amount?
opts: A. N500 which is the uncollectible amount for 0-30 days only
B. N1,500 which is the sum of N500 and N1,000 for both aging categories
C. N1,000 which is the uncollectible amount for 31-60 days only
D. N2,500 which is 5% of the total accounts receivable

questionBank.q: When a specific customer's account is determined to be uncollectible and is written off, what is the correct journal entry?
opts: A. Debit Bad Debt Expense and Credit Accounts Receivable for the write-off amount
B. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts and Credit Accounts Receivable for the write-off amount
C. Debit Accounts Receivable and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts for the write-off amount
D. Debit Bad Debt Expense and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts for the write-off amount
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'As soon as it is proven that a specific customer's account receivable will be uncollectible, the amount should be deducted from the Accounts Receivable and charged to the Allowance for doubtful accounts.'

questionBank.q: What is the effect on the accounting equation when a company writes off an uncollectible account that was previously provided for?
opts: A. Assets decrease and equity decreases by the write-off amount
B. Assets decrease and liabilities decrease by the write-off amount
C. Assets decrease and equity increases by the write-off amount
D. There is no effect on total assets or equity
questionBank.exp: Writing off an account reduces accounts receivable (asset) and reduces the allowance for doubtful accounts (contra-asset) by the same amount. Total assets remain unchanged.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an implication of bad debts for a company's financial health?
opts: A. Bad debts increase the company's reported revenue and profitability
B. Bad debts can cause cash flow problems and negatively impact the bottom line
C. Bad debts are recorded as assets and improve the company's financial position
D. Bad debts have no impact on the company's financial statements
questionBank.exp: The manual states the implications of bad debts: '1. Causes cashflow problems, which may lead to bankruptcy. 2. Impacts the organization's bottom-line negatively, leading to losses which may erode the capital.'

questionBank.q: When a company recovers cash from an account that was previously written off, what is the correct accounting treatment?
opts: A. Reverse the write-off by reinstating the accounts receivable
B. Record the cash receipt and treat the recovery as income
C. Record the cash receipt and reduce the allowance for doubtful accounts
D. Record the cash receipt and increase the bad debt expense
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When cash is received from a previously written off account, you take it directly into income. It only records the cash receipt and treats the recovery as an income to be reported on the income statement.'

questionBank.q: Which method of estimating bad debts categorizes receivables based on how long they have been outstanding?
opts: A. The percentage of receivables method which applies a single rate to the total balance
B. The aging of accounts receivable method which applies different rates to different age categories
C. The direct write-off method which writes off debts only when they become uncollectible
D. The historical percentage method which uses past experience for the current year
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'This method categorizes accounts receivable based on the length of time they have been outstanding (aging schedule). Different percentages are applied to each age category.'

questionBank.q: A company has an Allowance for Doubtful Accounts with a credit balance of N2,000 before adjustment. The aging analysis indicates that the required allowance is N7,500. What is the adjusting entry?
opts: A. Debit Bad Debt Expense N5,500 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N5,500
B. Debit Bad Debt Expense N7,500 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N7,500
C. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N5,500 and Credit Bad Debt Expense N5,500
D. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N7,500 and Credit Bad Debt Expense N7,500
questionBank.exp: Required allowance is N7,500. Existing allowance is N2,000. Adjustment needed = N7,500 - N2,000 = N5,500.

questionBank.q: What is the effect on net income when a company records bad debt expense?
opts: A. Net income increases because bad debt expense is a revenue account
B. Net income decreases because bad debt expense is an operating expense
C. Net income is unaffected because bad debt expense is a contra-asset
D. Net income increases because bad debt expense reduces the company's tax liability
questionBank.exp: Bad debt expense is an operating expense. Increasing expenses decreases net income.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct presentation of the allowance for doubtful accounts on the Statement of Financial Position?
opts: A. As a current liability because it represents amounts owed to the company
B. As a deduction from accounts receivable to show net realizable value
C. As a separate asset account because it represents future recoveries
D. As a component of equity because it affects retained earnings
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The balance in Provision for Bad debt is always deducted from the balance of the Accounts Receivable on the statement of financial position.'

questionBank.q: Which accounting concept is primarily supported by creating an allowance for doubtful accounts?
opts: A. The historical cost concept which requires assets to be recorded at cost
B. The matching principle which matches expenses with the revenues they help generate
C. The entity assumption which separates the business from its owners
D. The money measurement assumption which requires monetary expression
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Creating an allowance for doubtful accounts helps in adhering to the matching principle, as it aligns bad debt expenses with the revenues they helped generate.'

questionBank.q: A company has accounts receivable of N150,000 and an allowance for doubtful accounts of N5,000. What is the net realizable value of accounts receivable?
opts: A. N150,000 which is the gross accounts receivable balance
B. N145,000 which is the gross balance less the allowance
C. N155,000 which is the gross balance plus the allowance
D. N5,000 which is the allowance for doubtful accounts
questionBank.exp: Net realizable value = Accounts Receivable - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts = N150,000 - N5,000 = N145,000.

questionBank.q: When a company recovers a previously written-off account, what is the effect on the accounting equation at the time of cash receipt?
opts: A. Assets increase and liabilities decrease for the recovery amount
B. Assets increase and equity increases for the recovery amount
C. Assets decrease and equity decreases for the recovery amount
D. Assets decrease and liabilities increase for the recovery amount
questionBank.exp: Recording the cash receipt increases cash (asset) and increases income (equity). The manual states: 'It only records the cash receipt and treats the recovery as an income to be reported on the income statement.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of the direct write-off method for bad debts?
opts: A. Estimating bad debts as a percentage of credit sales at year-end
B. Writing off a customer's account only after it is determined to be uncollectible
C. Creating an allowance for doubtful accounts based on an aging schedule
D. Recording bad debts as a contra-asset against accounts receivable
questionBank.exp: The direct write-off method records bad debts only when a specific account is determined to be uncollectible, rather than estimating the allowance in advance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a method used to estimate bad debts?
opts: A. Percentage of receivables method based on a single rate applied to the total balance
B. Aging of accounts receivable method based on different rates for different age categories
C. Percentage of sales method based on historical credit sales experience
D. Market value method based on the current market value of receivables
questionBank.exp: The manual discusses the percentage of receivables method and the aging of accounts receivable method. Market value is not used to estimate bad debts.

questionBank.q: A company has an Allowance for Doubtful Accounts with a debit balance of N500 before adjustment. The aging analysis indicates that the required allowance is N6,000. What is the adjusting entry?
opts: A. Debit Bad Debt Expense N5,500 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N5,500
B. Debit Bad Debt Expense N6,000 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N6,000
C. Debit Bad Debt Expense N6,500 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N6,500
D. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N6,500 and Credit Bad Debt Expense N6,500
questionBank.exp: Required allowance is N6,000. Existing allowance has a debit balance of N500 (which means a credit of N500 is needed to bring it to zero, plus N6,000 to reach the required balance). Total credit needed = N6,000 + N500 = N6,500.

questionBank.q: What is the primary implication of the prudential guidelines on risk asset classification for banks?
opts: A. Banks must classify all loans as performing assets regardless of payment status
B. Banks must adopt the aging of accounts receivable method for provisioning
C. Banks must classify risk assets based on their geographical location
D. Banks must maintain a fixed percentage of all assets as loan loss provisions
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The prudential guidelines on risk asset classification and provisioning used in banking adopts the aging of accounts receivable method.'

questionBank.q: When a company writes off an uncollectible account, which of the following accounts is NOT affected?
opts: A. Accounts Receivable which is reduced by the write-off amount
B. Allowance for Doubtful Accounts which is reduced by the write-off amount
C. Bad Debt Expense which is recorded for the period of the write-off
D. Cash which is not affected by the write-off transaction
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The write-off reduces the gross accounts receivable and the allowance for bad debts without impacting the current period's profit.' Bad debt expense is not affected by the write-off if the allowance already exists.

questionBank.q: Why is it important for banks to properly estimate and provide for potential bad debts?
opts: A. To increase the bank's reported profits for the period
B. To ensure the bank holds enough capital to cover potential losses
C. To reduce the bank's tax liability by recognizing maximum expenses
D. To eliminate the need for regulatory oversight of loan quality
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Banks need to estimate potential losses (provision for bad debts) to ensure they hold enough capital to cover these losses, which is vital for maintaining financial stability and meeting regulatory requirements.'

questionBank.q: A company's accounts receivable aging schedule shows the following: 0-30 days: N100,000 (2% uncollectible), 31-60 days: N30,000 (5% uncollectible), 61-90 days: N10,000 (10% uncollectible). What is the total estimated uncollectible amount?
opts: A. N2,000 which is the uncollectible amount for 0-30 days only
B. N3,500 which is the sum of all three aging categories
C. N4,500 which is the sum of N2,000, N1,500, and N1,000
D. N5,000 which is 5% of the total accounts receivable

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the correct entry when a company recovers N17,200,000 from a previously written-off loan?
opts: A. Debit Cash N17,200,000 and Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N17,200,000
B. Debit Cash N17,200,000 and Credit Loans Recovered (Income) N17,200,000
C. Debit Accounts Receivable N17,200,000 and Credit Cash N17,200,000
D. Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts N17,200,000 and Credit Cash N17,200,000
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'When cash is received from a previously written off account, you take it directly into income. Debit Cash... Credit Loans Recovered (Income).'

questionBank.q: What is the effect on the accounting equation when a company recovers a previously written-off account and records it as income?
opts: A. Assets increase and liabilities decrease for the recovery amount
B. Assets decrease and equity decreases for the recovery amount
C. Assets increase and equity increases for the recovery amount
D. Liabilities increase and equity increases for the recovery amount
questionBank.exp: Cash (asset) increases and income (equity) increases. The manual states: 'It only records the cash receipt and treats the recovery as an income to be reported on the income statement.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a direct consequence of having a high level of bad debts for a business?
opts: A. Cash flow problems that may lead to bankruptcy
B. Erosion of capital due to losses from uncollectible accounts
C. Negative impact on the company's reputation with shareholders
D. Increased market value of the company's shares
questionBank.exp: Bad debts negatively impact a company's financial health and reputation. They would not increase the market value of shares.

questionBank.q: The aging of accounts receivable method is considered more accurate than the percentage of receivables method because it:
opts: A. Applies a single rate to all accounts receivable regardless of age
B. Uses historical data from the company's past experience with bad debts
C. Considers the different risk levels of receivables based on how long they are outstanding
D. Requires less detailed information about individual customer accounts
questionBank.exp: The aging method applies different percentages to different age categories, recognizing that older receivables are generally more likely to be uncollectible.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as a tangible non-current asset?
opts: A. Goodwill which represents the premium paid for a business over its net assets
B. Patents which provide exclusive rights to use an invention
C. Machinery which is used in the production process of the business
D. Copyrights which protect literary and artistic works
questionBank.exp: Tangible non-current assets have physical substance. Machinery is a tangible asset. Goodwill, patents, and copyrights are intangible assets.

questionBank.q: Which of the following costs would be included in the acquisition cost of a non-current asset?
opts: A. The purchase price of the asset only, excluding all other costs
B. The purchase price plus delivery, installation, and legal fees related to the acquisition
C. The purchase price plus any costs incurred after the asset is placed in service
D. The purchase price plus the estimated salvage value of the asset
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The acquisition cost of a non-current asset typically includes the following components: Purchase Price, Delivery Costs, Installation Costs, Legal and Title Fees, Testing and Inspection Costs.'

questionBank.q: A company purchases machinery for N50,000, pays N2,000 for shipping, N5,000 for installation, and N1,500 in legal fees. What is the total acquisition cost?
opts: A. N50,000 which is the purchase price of the machinery
B. N58,500 which is the sum of all costs associated with the acquisition
C. N55,000 which excludes the legal fees from the total cost
D. N52,000 which excludes the shipping and legal fees
questionBank.exp: Acquisition cost = Purchase Price N50,000 + Delivery N2,000 + Installation N5,000 + Legal Fees N1,500 = N58,500.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as a capital expenditure?
opts: A. Routine repairs to keep equipment in working condition
B. Salaries and wages of administrative staff
C. Advertising costs incurred to promote the company's products
D. Purchase of a new building for business operations
questionBank.exp: Capital expenditures are investments in long-term assets. The manual's illustration shows: 'Buying van - Capital,' 'Putting extra headlights on van - Capital,' and 'Buying machinery - Capital.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as a revenue expenditure?
opts: A. The purchase of a new vehicle for the sales team
B. The cost of petrol and routine maintenance for company vehicles
C. The purchase of land for future business expansion
D. The installation of a new computer system
