questionBank.exp: Revenue expenditures are day-to-day operating expenses. The manual shows: 'Petrol costs of van - Revenue,' 'Repairs to van - Revenue,' and 'Electricity costs of using machinery - Revenue.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of depreciation?
opts: A. Physical deterioration through wear and tear
B. Economic obsolescence due to changing market conditions
C. The passage of time for assets with legal rights
D. The payment of dividends to shareholders
questionBank.exp: The manual lists causes of depreciation: Physical Deterioration, Economic obsolescence, Functional obsolescence, Expiration of legal rights, Time, and Depletion. Dividends are distributions to shareholders, not a cause of depreciation.

questionBank.q: Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation expense for an asset costing N100,000 with a residual value of N10,000 and a useful life of 5 years?
opts: A. N20,000 which is the cost divided by the useful life of 5 years
B. N18,000 which is the cost less residual value divided by 5 years
C. N22,000 which is the cost plus residual value divided by 5 years
D. N10,000 which is the residual value of the asset
questionBank.exp: Depreciation expense = (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life = (N100,000 - N10,000) / 5 = N90,000 / 5 = N18,000 per year.

questionBank.q: Under the reducing balance method, if a machine costing N100,000 is depreciated at 20% per year, what is the depreciation expense for the second year?
opts: A. N20,000 which is 20% of the original cost
B. N16,000 which is 20% of the net book value after year one
C. N25,600 which is 20% of the net book value after year two
D. N12,800 which is 20% of the net book value after year three

questionBank.q: A company purchased equipment for N60,000 with a useful life of 4 years and no residual value. Using the straight-line method, what is the accumulated depreciation after 3 years?
opts: A. N15,000 which is the annual depreciation for one year
B. N45,000 which is the annual depreciation of N15,000 multiplied by 3 years
C. N60,000 which is the full cost of the asset
D. N30,000 which is the annual depreciation for two years
questionBank.exp: Annual depreciation = N60,000 / 4 = N15,000. After 3 years, accumulated depreciation = N15,000 × 3 = N45,000.

questionBank.q: Which depreciation method allocates a higher depreciation expense in the early years of an asset's life?
opts: A. The straight-line method which allocates equal expense each year
B. The reducing balance method which charges a fixed percentage of the net book value
C. The units of production method based on actual output or usage
D. The amortization method used for intangible assets
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'This method allocates a higher depreciation expense in the early years of an asset's life and decreases it in subsequent years. It is also known as the Declining Balance, Accelerated Depreciation.'

questionBank.q: Using the units of production method, what is the depreciation expense for an asset costing N50,000 with a residual value of N5,000, total estimated production of 100,000 units, and actual production of 20,000 units in year one?
opts: B. N10,000 which is N50,000 / 100,000 units × 20,000 units
C. N8,000 which is N50,000 / 100,000 units × 16,000 units
questionBank.exp: Depreciation rate per unit = (Cost - Residual Value) / Total Units = (N50,000 - N5,000) / 100,000 = N0.45 per unit. Depreciation expense = 20,000 units × N0.45 = N9,000.

questionBank.q: When a company sells equipment, which of the following is the correct accounting entry to record the removal of the asset and its accumulated depreciation?
opts: A. Debit Cash, Credit Equipment, and Credit Gain on Disposal for the sale
B. Debit Accumulated Depreciation, Credit Equipment, and Debit/Credit Gain/Loss on Disposal
C. Debit Equipment, Credit Accumulated Depreciation, and Credit Cash for the sale
D. Debit Gain on Disposal, Credit Equipment, and Credit Accumulated Depreciation
questionBank.exp: To remove the asset, debit accumulated depreciation (to remove the contra-asset balance) and credit the asset account (to remove the original cost). The difference is recorded as a gain or loss.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is correct about asset revaluation?
opts: A. A revaluation surplus is recorded as an expense in the income statement
B. A revaluation deficit is recorded in the revaluation surplus under equity
C. A revaluation surplus is recorded in the revaluation surplus account under shareholders' equity
D. A revaluation deficit is recorded as a gain in the income statement
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Revaluation Surplus: If the fair value of an asset exceeds its carrying value after revaluation. The surplus is recorded in the revaluation surplus account under shareholders' equity.'

questionBank.q: Lehman Pharmaceutical Limited sells equipment for N7,000,000 at the end of its 16th year. The equipment cost N25,000,000 with a useful life of 20 years and no residual value using straight-line depreciation. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
opts: A. A gain of N2,000,000 because the sale proceeds exceed the carrying value
B. A loss of N2,000,000 because the sale proceeds are less than the carrying value
C. A gain of N7,000,000 because the sale proceeds are the full amount received
D. A loss of N25,000,000 because the asset was sold for less than its cost
questionBank.exp: Annual depreciation = N25,000,000 / 20 = N1,250,000. After 16 years, accumulated depreciation = N1,250,000 × 16 = N20,000,000. Carrying value = N25,000,000 - N20,000,000 = N5,000,000. Gain = N7,000,000 - N5,000,000 = N2,000,000.

questionBank.q: What is the correct journal entry to record depreciation expense for a building?
opts: A. Debit Depreciation Expense and Credit Building for the depreciation amount
B. Debit Depreciation Expense and Credit Accumulated Depreciation for the depreciation amount
C. Debit Accumulated Depreciation and Credit Depreciation Expense for the depreciation amount
D. Debit Building and Credit Depreciation Expense for the depreciation amount
questionBank.exp: Depreciation is recorded by debiting Depreciation Expense and crediting Accumulated Depreciation. The building account itself is not directly credited.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for properly valuing and accounting for non-current assets?
opts: A. Accurate financial reporting to investors and creditors
B. Proper matching of expenses with revenues over time
C. Maximizing the company's reported profits by inflating asset values
D. Tax implications and compliance with tax regulations
questionBank.exp: The manual states proper valuation is important for 'Accurate Financial Reporting,' 'Income Recognition,' 'Taxation,' and 'Asset Management.' Inflating asset values would be fraudulent and not a legitimate reason.

questionBank.q: A company revalues an asset from a carrying value of N70,000 to a fair value of N120,000. What is the journal entry for the revaluation surplus?
opts: A. Debit Revaluation Surplus N50,000 and Credit Asset Account N50,000
B. Debit Asset Account N50,000 and Credit Revaluation Surplus N50,000
C. Debit Asset Account N50,000 and Credit Retained Earnings N50,000
D. Debit Retained Earnings N50,000 and Credit Asset Account N50,000
questionBank.exp: When an asset is revalued upward, the asset account is debited (increased) and the revaluation surplus (equity) is credited.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about the difference between capital and revenue expenditure?
opts: A. Capital expenditure is recognized as an expense in the period it is incurred
B. Revenue expenditure is added to the value of non-current assets on the balance sheet
C. Capital expenditure increases the company's assets and affects the income statement through depreciation
D. Revenue expenditure is capitalized and depreciated over the asset's useful life
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Capital expenditures increase the company's assets on the balance sheet and affect the income statement indirectly through depreciation or amortization expenses. Revenue expenditures are fully recognized as operating expenses on the income statement.'

questionBank.q: What is the amortization of an intangible asset?
opts: A. The systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life
B. The systematic and periodic allocation of the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life
C. The allocation of the cost of natural resources over time
D. The process of increasing the value of an asset to its market value
questionBank.exp: The manual distinguishes: 'Amortization refers to the systematic and periodic spreading of the cost of an intangible asset over that asset's useful life.'

questionBank.q: A company spends N1,500 on machinery: N1,000 for an improvement and N500 for repairs. How should this be classified?
opts: A. N1,500 as capital expenditure because it relates to machinery
B. N1,000 as capital expenditure and N500 as revenue expenditure
C. N500 as capital expenditure and N1,000 as revenue expenditure
D. N1,500 as revenue expenditure because it is a cost of maintaining the asset
questionBank.exp: The manual's illustration shows: 'We spent a N1,500 on machinery: N1,000 Capital N1,000 was for an item (improvement) added to the machine; and N500 was for repairs - Revenue.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of an intangible non-current asset?
opts: A. Goodwill which represents the premium paid for a business acquisition
B. Patents which provide exclusive rights to use an invention
C. Motor vehicles which are used for business transportation
D. Trademarks which protect brand names and logos
questionBank.exp: Motor vehicles are tangible non-current assets. Goodwill, patents, and trademarks are intangible assets that lack physical substance.

questionBank.q: What is the formula for calculating the reducing balance depreciation rate when the salvage value and useful life are known?
opts: A. R = 1 - √(C/S) which uses the cost and salvage value
B. R = 1 - √(S/C) which uses the salvage value and cost ratio
C. R = (C - S) / N which is the straight-line rate
D. R = S / C which is the salvage value divided by the cost
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The basic formula used to find the Depreciation Rate to apply with this method is: R = 1 - √(S/C) where R = Declining Rate, N = Useful Life, S = Salvage Value, C = Acquisition Cost.'

questionBank.q: What is depletion in accounting?
opts: A. The allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life
B. The systematic and periodic allocation of the cost of an intangible asset
C. The allocation of the cost of natural resources over time
D. The process of reducing the value of an asset for tax purposes
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Depletion refers to the allocation of the cost of natural resources over time. For example, an oil well has a finite life before all the oil is pumped out.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly describes the treatment of a revaluation deficit?
opts: A. The deficit is recorded in the revaluation surplus account under equity
B. The deficit is recognized in the income statement and reduces retained earnings
C. The deficit is deferred and recognized over the remaining useful life of the asset
D. The deficit is ignored and does not affect the financial statements
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'Revaluation Deficit: If the fair value of an asset is less than its carrying value after revaluation, the deficit is recognized in the income statement. It reduces retained earnings.'

questionBank.q: Why is the units of production method considered more appropriate than straight-line depreciation for certain types of assets?
opts: A. It provides a consistent depreciation expense each year regardless of usage
B. It matches the depreciation expense with the actual usage and output of the asset
C. It allocates higher depreciation in the early years and lower in later years
D. It requires no estimate of the asset's useful life or residual value
questionBank.exp: The manual states: 'The Units of Production Method... is a depreciation method used to allocate the cost of an asset over its useful life based on the number of units or activity it produces. This method is particularly useful when an asset's usage varies from year to year.'

questionBank.q: In a partnership, how are profits and losses typically allocated among the partners?
opts: A. According to the partnership agreement, which the partners adopt voluntarily
B. According to a fixed percentage set by the corporation's board of directors annually
C. According to the proportion of shares each partner holds in the public market
D. According to the legal default set by the tax authority for all partnerships
questionBank.exp: Partnerships allocate profits and losses according to terms the partners agree upon themselves, not a board-imposed rate, share-market proportion, or statutory default.

questionBank.q: Which feature distinguishes the governance structure of a corporation from that of a sole proprietorship?
opts: A. A corporation governs through a single owner who makes all major decisions alone
B. A corporation governs through a board of directors and officers in a formal structure
C. A corporation governs through a partnership agreement signed by all shareholders
D. A corporation governs through informal arrangements similar to a sole trader's business
questionBank.exp: Corporations have a formal governance structure with a board of directors and officers, unlike the single-owner control of a sole proprietorship.

questionBank.q: Which business structure exposes its owner to unlimited personal liability for business debts?
opts: A. A corporation, where shareholders enjoy limited liability protection for their investment
B. A limited liability company, where members enjoy protection similar to corporations
C. A sole proprietorship, where the owner has no liability protection from business debts
D. A public company, where shareholders are shielded from creditors by company law
questionBank.exp: Sole proprietors have unlimited personal liability for business debts, unlike corporations, LLCs, and public companies, which offer limited liability protection to their owners.

questionBank.q: According to the AICPA, accounting is best described as which type of activity?
opts: A. A regulatory activity that enforces compliance with taxation and reporting laws
B. A clerical activity that simply records transactions without further analysis
C. A managerial activity that sets company strategy and long-term business goals
D. A service activity that provides quantitative financial information for economic decisions
questionBank.exp: The AICPA defines accounting as 'a service activity whose function is to provide quantitative information...intended to be useful in making economic decisions.'

questionBank.q: Why is accounting often referred to as the 'language of business'?
opts: A. Because it is the system through which financial information is communicated to users
B. Because it uses Latin terminology that is universally taught in business schools
C. Because every country requires it to be reported in a single global currency
D. Because it was the first subject formally taught in business administration programs
questionBank.exp: Accounting is called the language of business because it is the system through which financial information about an entity is measured and communicated to its users.

questionBank.q: What is the key difference between bookkeeping and the broader accounting process?
opts: A. Bookkeeping focuses on reporting to investors, while accounting only records daily transactions
B. Bookkeeping focuses on recording transactions, while accounting also includes analysis and reporting
C. Bookkeeping is performed by auditors, while accounting is performed by company managers
D. Bookkeeping applies only to corporations, while accounting applies to all business types
questionBank.exp: Bookkeeping is the recording function within the broader accounting process, which also includes summarizing and reporting financial information.

questionBank.q: Why would a government regulatory agency be considered a user of a company's accounting information?
opts: A. To assist the company in setting its internal pricing strategy for products
B. To help the company recruit qualified accounting and finance staff
C. To assess the company's compliance with tax laws and other regulatory requirements
D. To advise the company on which suppliers to use for raw materials
questionBank.exp: Government agencies and regulators use accounting information primarily to assess a company's compliance with tax laws and other regulatory requirements.

questionBank.q: How does the chosen business structure typically affect a company's exit strategy?
opts: A. Selling a corporation requires dissolving the entire legal structure before any transfer occurs
B. Selling a partnership always requires shareholder approval through a formal stock exchange
C. Selling a sole proprietorship requires transferring shares to existing business partners
D. Selling a corporation involves transferring shares, while a partnership may involve selling interests
questionBank.exp: The manual notes that exit strategies differ by structure: selling a corporation involves transferring shares, while partnerships may involve selling ownership interests.

questionBank.q: What does 'pass-through taxation' mean for a sole proprietorship or partnership?
opts: A. Profits and losses pass directly to the owners' personal tax returns for taxation
B. Profits are taxed once at the corporate level before being distributed to owners
C. Losses are passed to the government as tax credits for future business use
D. Profits pass through an escrow account before being reported to tax authorities
questionBank.exp: Pass-through taxation means that profits and losses flow directly to the owners' personal tax returns, avoiding taxation at the business level.

questionBank.q: Which statement correctly describes how business entity type can influence accounting method choice?
opts: A. Corporations must use cash-basis accounting, while sole proprietorships use accrual exclusively
B. Sole proprietorships and partnerships may use cash or accrual, while corporations typically use accrual
C. All business entities are legally required to use accrual-basis accounting regardless of size
D. Partnerships must use cash-basis accounting, while corporations may choose either method freely
questionBank.exp: Sole proprietorships and partnerships may opt for cash or accrual accounting, while corporations typically use accrual accounting for financial reporting.

questionBank.q: How do ownership structures typically differ between a corporation and a partnership?
opts: A. Corporations allocate interests per agreement, while partnerships issue shares of stock
B. Both corporations and partnerships issue identical units of stock to their owners
C. Corporations issue shares of stock, while partnerships allocate interests per their agreement
D. Neither corporations nor partnerships have a formal method for allocating ownership
questionBank.exp: Corporations issue shares of stock to represent ownership, while partnerships allocate ownership interests based on the terms of their partnership agreement.

questionBank.q: Compared to sole proprietorships, why do corporations face more stringent financial reporting requirements?
opts: A. Corporations are exempt from regulatory oversight due to their separate legal status
B. Corporations only report financial information when requested by their own employees
C. Corporations are required to report finances solely to their own internal management team
D. Corporations must produce audited statements for shareholders and regulators they answer to
questionBank.exp: Corporations face more stringent reporting requirements because they must produce audited financial statements for shareholders and regulators.

questionBank.q: How does basic accounting knowledge specifically help bank staff with risk management?
opts: A. It helps staff identify and manage financial risks tied to products and services offered
B. It allows staff to bypass internal audit checks when reviewing customer transactions
C. It enables staff to set the bank's overall capital adequacy ratio independently
D. It permits staff to approve large loans without further managerial review or oversight
questionBank.exp: Accounting knowledge helps bank staff identify and manage the financial risks associated with the variety of products and services banks offer.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best contrasts the AAA and AICPA definitions of accounting?
opts: A. The AAA emphasizes service activity for decisions; the AICPA emphasizes identifying information
B. The AAA emphasizes the process of identifying and measuring information; the AICPA emphasizes its service nature
C. The AAA and AICPA definitions both focus exclusively on the preparation of tax returns
D. The AAA and AICPA definitions both define accounting as a purely clerical recording function
questionBank.exp: The AAA frames accounting around identifying, measuring, and communicating information, while the AICPA frames it as a service activity supporting economic decisions.

questionBank.q: How does personal liability typically compare between a sole proprietorship and a general partnership?
opts: A. Sole proprietors face unlimited liability, while general partners enjoy limited liability protection
B. General partners face unlimited liability, while sole proprietors enjoy limited liability protection
C. Both sole proprietors and general partners typically face unlimited personal liability for debts
D. Neither sole proprietors nor general partners are personally liable for business debts incurred
questionBank.exp: Both sole proprietors and general partners typically bear unlimited personal liability for the debts of the business, unlike shareholders in a corporation.

questionBank.q: What does 'share premium' represent in a company's equity section?
opts: A. The amount of dividends declared but not yet paid to ordinary shareholders
B. The total nominal value of all shares authorized for issuance by the company
C. The amount of retained earnings set aside for future expansion projects
D. The amount received from shareholders in excess of the nominal value of shares issued
questionBank.exp: Share premium is the money a company raises in excess of the nominal value of the shares it issues to shareholders.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best defines 'retained earnings' in a company's equity?
opts: A. The portion of cumulative profit retained in the business rather than distributed to shareholders
B. The total cash balance held by the company at its various bank accounts
C. The total amount of share capital that has been called up by the company
D. The portion of revenue collected from customers but not yet recognized as earned
questionBank.exp: Retained earnings are the portion of a company's cumulative profit that is retained and saved for future use rather than distributed to shareholders.

questionBank.q: A revaluation reserve arises in a company's equity when which of the following occurs?
opts: A. A company writes off a customer's account as permanently uncollectible
B. An asset's fair value is assessed and found to exceed its existing carrying value
C. A company pays a cash dividend that reduces the retained earnings balance
D. A company issues new shares at a price equal to their nominal value
questionBank.exp: A revaluation reserve arises when an asset's fair value, on reassessment, exceeds its existing carrying value on the books.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified under operating activities in the Statement of Cash Flows?
opts: A. Proceeds received from the issue of new ordinary shares to investors
B. Cash paid to acquire a piece of machinery for the production process
C. Profit before tax adjusted for non-cash items such as depreciation and amortisation
D. Cash received from the disposal of shares held in another company
questionBank.exp: Operating activities begin with profit before tax, adjusted for non-cash items such as depreciation and amortisation, as shown in the manual's cash flow elements.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified under investing activities in the Statement of Cash Flows?
opts: A. Cash received from customers for goods sold during the period
B. Cash paid to settle wages owed to employees for the period
C. Cash received from a bank loan taken out during the period
D. Cash paid to purchase debentures issued by another company
questionBank.exp: The purchase of debentures in another company is an investing activity, distinct from the operating items of customer receipts and wage payments, and the financing item of a bank loan.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified under financing activities in the Statement of Cash Flows?
opts: A. Proceeds received from the issue of shares to new investors during the period
B. Cash paid to acquire shares in another company as a long-term investment
C. Depreciation and amortisation charged against profit for the period
D. Cash received from the disposal of fixed assets no longer in use
questionBank.exp: Proceeds from issuing shares represent a financing activity, as they relate to the company's capital structure rather than its operations or investments.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a stated purpose of the Notes to the Financial Statements?
opts: A. To replace the need for a separate Statement of Financial Position entirely
B. To present information about the basis of preparation and specific accounting policies used
C. To provide a forecast of the company's expected revenue for the next five years
D. To list the personal addresses of all the company's directors and shareholders
questionBank.exp: The notes should present information about the basis of preparation of the financial statements and the specific accounting policies used, not replace any primary statement.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified as a current asset on the Statement of Financial Position?
opts: A. A 20-year-old factory building used for ongoing manufacturing operations
B. A trademark with an indefinite useful life held by the company
C. Trade receivables expected to be collected within the next twelve months
D. A piece of machinery expected to be used for the next eight years
questionBank.exp: Trade receivables expected to be collected within twelve months are a current asset, unlike the building, trademark, and machinery, which are non-current assets.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified as a non-current liability?
opts: A. Accounts payable for inventory due to be paid within the next thirty days
B. Bank overdraft repayable immediately upon the bank's demand for funds
C. Accrued wages owed to staff for the final week of the financial year
D. A debenture due for repayment in eight years from the reporting date
questionBank.exp: A debenture repayable in eight years is a non-current liability, while the other items are all current liabilities due within a year.

questionBank.q: Under IFRS, which of the following is required as part of a complete set of financial statements?
opts: A. A Statement of Changes in Equity reconciling movements in equity balances
B. A Statement of Marketing Expenditure detailing the company's advertising spend
C. A Statement of Employee Headcount detailing staffing changes during the year
D. A Statement of Competitor Analysis comparing the company to industry rivals
questionBank.exp: IFRS requires a Statement of Changes in Equity as one of the five components of a complete set of financial statements; none of the other listed statements are recognized components.

questionBank.q: How are dividends treated within the Statement of Changes in Equity?
opts: A. As an inflow that increases the share capital balance for the period
B. As an outflow that reduces the retained earnings balance for the period
C. As an expense that reduces gross profit in the trading account
D. As a liability that is added to the non-current liabilities section
questionBank.exp: Dividends are shown as an outflow within the Statement of Changes in Equity, reducing the retained earnings balance, rather than as an income statement expense.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a recognized component of the Statement of Changes in Equity?
opts: A. Cost of sales deducted from revenue to determine gross profit
B. Carriage inwards added to the cost of purchases for the period
C. Transfers to or from reserves made during the reporting period
D. Bank charges deducted by the bank but unrecorded in the cash book
questionBank.exp: Transfers to or from reserves are listed among the components of retained earnings within the Statement of Changes in Equity.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best represents the equity section of the Statement of Financial Position?
opts: A. Current and non-current liabilities, representing amounts owed to outsiders
B. Current and non-current assets, representing items the business owns
C. Notes and disclosures, representing additional non-quantitative information
D. Share capital and reserves, representing the owners' stake in the business
questionBank.exp: The equity section of the Statement of Financial Position consists of share capital and reserves, representing the owners' stake in the business.

questionBank.q: Under the Statement of Profit or Loss, which of the following would be classified as 'other income'?
opts: A. Income earned from a source outside of the company's core trading operations
B. Revenue generated from the company's primary trading activities during the period
C. Cost of sales deducted from revenue to calculate the gross profit figure
D. Administrative expenses incurred in running the company's head office
questionBank.exp: Other income refers to income earned from sources outside of the company's primary trading activities, distinguishing it from revenue.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would be classified under 'selling and distribution' expenses in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
opts: A. The cost of goods purchased specifically for resale to customers
B. The cost of delivering finished goods to customers after a sale is made
C. The cost of raw materials consumed in the manufacturing process
D. The cost of interest paid on a long-term loan from the bank
questionBank.exp: Carriage outwards, the cost of delivering goods to customers after a sale, is classified as a selling and distribution expense.

questionBank.q: If a company is legally permitted to issue 2 million shares but has only issued 1.2 million, what is the authorized share capital based on?
opts: A. The 1.2 million shares that have actually been distributed to shareholders
B. The 800,000 shares that remain unissued and available for future sale
C. The 2 million shares the company is legally allowed to issue under its registration
D. The portion of the 1.2 million shares that have been fully paid for by holders
questionBank.exp: Authorized share capital is the total number of shares a company is legally permitted to issue, regardless of how many have actually been issued.

questionBank.q: What does 'uncalled capital' represent for a company with partly paid issued shares?
opts: A. The amount of share capital that the company is legally barred from ever issuing
B. The amount that shareholders have already paid in full for their issued shares
C. The amount of dividends that have been declared but not yet distributed to holders
D. The amount still to be received in future on issued shares that has not yet been demanded
questionBank.exp: Uncalled capital is the amount still to be received in future on issued shares, representing the portion that has not yet been formally called for.

questionBank.q: Why is the Statement of Financial Position described as a 'snapshot' rather than a record over time?
opts: A. Because it reports balances of assets, liabilities, and equity as at one specific date
B. Because it summarizes income and expenses accumulated over an entire trading period
C. Because it reconciles the opening and closing cash balances for the period
D. Because it reports movements in equity accounts across several reporting periods
questionBank.exp: The Statement of Financial Position reports balances as at a particular point in time, which is why it is described using the phrase 'as at' rather than 'for the year ended.'

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five components of a complete set of financial statements under IFRS?
opts: A. The Statement of Cash Flows summarising inflows and outflows of cash
B. The Statement of Departmental Budgets detailing planned expenditure
C. The Statement of Changes in Equity reconciling movements in equity
D. The Statement of Profit or Loss detailing financial performance
questionBank.exp: A Statement of Departmental Budgets is not one of the five IFRS components; the cash flows, changes in equity, and profit or loss statements are all required components.

questionBank.q: How does 'calls in arrears' differ from 'uncalled capital'?
opts: A. Calls in arrears has not yet been demanded; uncalled capital has been demanded but unpaid
B. Calls in arrears applies only to corporations; uncalled capital applies only to partnerships
C. Calls in arrears has been demanded but unpaid; uncalled capital has not yet been demanded
D. Calls in arrears represents paid-up capital; uncalled capital represents authorized capital
questionBank.exp: Calls in arrears is an amount that has been demanded but not paid, while uncalled capital has not yet been demanded at all.

questionBank.q: What is the key distinction between accounting assumptions and accounting concepts as discussed in the manual?
opts: A. Concepts are the foundational rules; assumptions are applied on the basis of those concepts
B. Assumptions apply only to small businesses; concepts apply only to large corporations
C. Assumptions are optional guidelines; concepts are mandatory legal requirements for all firms
D. Assumptions are the foundational rules; concepts are applied on the basis of those assumptions
questionBank.exp: Accounting concepts are applied on the basis of the foundational accounting assumptions, which provide the groundwork for consistent and reliable financial reporting.

questionBank.q: According to the manual, accounting assumptions are based on standards defined by which body?
opts: A. The Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria, which lays the groundwork for reliable reporting
B. The Central Bank of Nigeria, which regulates interest rates and monetary policy
C. The Nigerian Stock Exchange, which oversees the trading of public company shares
D. The Corporate Affairs Commission, which registers new companies and partnerships
questionBank.exp: The manual identifies the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria as the body whose standards underpin the major accounting assumptions.

questionBank.q: Why are accounting concepts important for comparing the financial statements of different companies?
opts: A. They allow each company to choose entirely different formats for clarity and flexibility
B. They bring standardization, preventing each business from using a unique reporting format
C. They eliminate the need for companies to follow any common reporting standards at all
D. They require companies to report only in the currency of their country of incorporation
questionBank.exp: Accounting concepts bring standardization to financial reporting, preventing each business from using its own peculiar format, which would make comparison difficult.

questionBank.q: Under the entity assumption, how is a sole trader's personal investment in the business treated in the books?
opts: A. As a gift to the business that creates no obligation for repayment to the proprietor
B. As income earned by the business from operations during the accounting period
C. As money given to the business, with the proprietor treated as a creditor of the business
D. As an expense incurred by the business in the course of normal trading activities
questionBank.exp: Under the entity assumption, money invested by a sole trader is treated as if it were given to the business, with the proprietor regarded as a creditor to the extent of that capital.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would NOT be recorded in the accounting books under the money measurement assumption?
opts: A. The purchase cost of a delivery van used by the business for operations
B. The amount of cash held by the business at its various bank accounts
C. The cost of raw materials purchased on credit from a regular supplier
D. The general health condition of the company's chairman and senior staff
questionBank.exp: The general health condition of company staff cannot be expressed in monetary terms and is therefore not recorded, unlike the van, cash, and raw material costs.

questionBank.q: If the going concern assumption did not apply to a business, what would happen to the current/non-current classification of assets?
opts: A. The classification would lose much of its significance under a liquidation approach
B. The classification would become more precise and easier for users to interpret
C. The classification would remain entirely unaffected by the change in assumption
D. The classification would automatically convert all assets into non-current assets
questionBank.exp: Without the going concern assumption, the current and non-current classification of assets and liabilities would lose much of its significance under a liquidation approach.

questionBank.q: According to the periodicity assumption, what trade-off do companies face when releasing financial information quickly?
opts: A. A trade-off between profitability and liquidity, as quicker reporting reduces available cash
B. A trade-off between relevance and reliability, as quicker information may include more errors
C. A trade-off between taxation and regulation, as quicker reporting increases tax liability
D. A trade-off between equity and debt financing, as quicker reporting affects capital structure
questionBank.exp: The periodicity assumption highlights a trade-off between relevance and reliability, since faster reporting of financial results increases the risk of error.

questionBank.q: Why does the historical cost principle prevent a company from recording an asset at its current inflated market value?
opts: A. Because current market values are always lower than the original purchase price
B. Because regulators require all assets to be insured at their original purchase price
C. Because historical cost supports conservative accounting and avoids overstating asset values
D. Because market values cannot legally be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements
questionBank.exp: The historical cost principle is in line with conservative accounting because it prevents the overstating of an asset's recorded value above its original cost.

questionBank.q: Under the revenue recognition principle, why might a company NOT record revenue at the point cash is received in advance?
opts: A. Because cash receipts are never recorded in the company's accounting records
B. Because revenue can only be recorded once a full year has elapsed from the date received
C. Because advance payments are automatically classified as a reduction in expenses
D. Because the earning process may not yet be substantially complete at that point
questionBank.exp: Revenue is not recognized at the point of advance receipt if the earning process is not yet substantially complete, since the risks and rewards of ownership have not transferred.

questionBank.q: Under the matching principle, when should a sales commission expense be recognized?
opts: A. In the same period as the sale that generated the commission, regardless of payment timing
B. Only in the period when the commission is actually paid in cash to the salesperson
C. Spread evenly across the entire financial year regardless of when sales occurred
D. In the period immediately following the one in which the related sale was made
questionBank.exp: Under the matching principle, a sales commission expense should be recognized in the same period as the sale that generated it, regardless of when it is actually paid.

questionBank.q: What is the central idea behind the substance over form principle?
opts: A. Financial statements should always follow the strict legal wording of every contract signed
B. Financial statements should reflect the economic reality of a transaction, not just its legal form
C. Financial statements should ignore economic reality in favour of consistent legal treatment
D. Financial statements should be prepared based only on verbal agreements between parties
questionBank.exp: Substance over form requires financial statements to reflect the economic reality of a transaction rather than merely its legal form.

questionBank.q: According to the full disclosure principle, how should material information be treated if it cannot be included directly in the financial statements?
opts: A. It should be omitted entirely since it cannot fit within the prescribed format
B. It should be reported only to the company's external auditors and no one else
C. It should be shown as a footnote after the financial reports for users to review
D. It should be delayed and disclosed only in the following year's financial statements
questionBank.exp: If material information cannot be included directly within the financial reports, the full disclosure principle requires it to be shown as a footnote.

questionBank.q: Why might the same dollar amount be considered material for a small business but immaterial for a large corporation?
opts: A. Materiality is fixed at a universal monetary threshold set by international law
B. Materiality applies only to corporations and never to small businesses
C. Materiality is determined solely by the age of the business since incorporation
D. Materiality depends on the relative size and scope of the business in question
questionBank.exp: What counts as material differs based on the size and scope of the firm in question, rather than being fixed at a universal threshold.

questionBank.q: How does the prudence principle guard against the overstatement of a company's financial position?
opts: A. By ensuring that income and assets are not recorded above a cautious, realistic estimate
B. By requiring that all assets be valued at their highest possible market estimate
C. By allowing companies to recognize anticipated profits before contracts are finalized
D. By eliminating the need for companies to provide for any doubtful debts at all
questionBank.exp: The prudence principle ensures that income and assets are not overstated, guarding against an overly optimistic picture of a company's financial position.

questionBank.q: Under the accrual principle, expenses are recognized based on which of the following?
opts: A. The period in which cash is paid, regardless of when they are incurred
B. The period in which they are incurred, regardless of when cash is paid
C. The period chosen at the company's discretion for tax minimisation purposes
D. The period in which the related asset is eventually disposed of by the company
questionBank.exp: Under the accrual principle, expenses are recognized in the period in which they are incurred, not necessarily when cash is actually paid.

questionBank.q: Which accounting assumption justifies treating a sole trader's business as separate from the trader personally, even though no legal separation exists?
opts: A. The going concern assumption, which assumes the business will continue operating indefinitely
B. The periodicity assumption, which splits the business's life into artificial time periods
C. The entity assumption, which applies for accounting purposes despite the lack of legal separation
D. The money measurement assumption, which requires all transactions to be expressed monetarily
questionBank.exp: The entity assumption applies to sole traders for accounting purposes even though no legal separation exists between the trader and the business, unlike for a body corporate.

questionBank.q: Why does the monetary unit assumption rely on the more basic assumption that quantitative data is useful?
opts: A. Because without quantitative usefulness, expressing transactions in money would serve no purpose for decisions
B. Because monetary units must first be converted into foreign currency before being recorded
C. Because quantitative data is only useful once a business has ceased all its operations
D. Because monetary assumptions apply only to assets and never to liabilities or expenses
questionBank.exp: The application of the money measurement assumption depends on the more basic assumption that quantitative data is useful in communicating information and supporting rational decisions.

questionBank.q: Which of the following situations represents the only scenario where the going concern assumption becomes inapplicable?
opts: A. When a company experiences a temporary decline in sales for one quarter
B. When liquidation of the business appears imminent and unavoidable
C. When a company changes its accounting period from monthly to quarterly
D. When a company's assets increase in value due to favourable market conditions
questionBank.exp: The going concern assumption applies in most business situations and is only inapplicable where liquidation appears imminent.

questionBank.q: What does the periodicity assumption require regarding the allocation of expenses?
opts: A. It requires allocation only at the point a company is preparing for final liquidation
B. It requires allocation of expenses between capital and revenue across artificial time periods
C. It requires that no expenses be allocated until the entire business cycle is complete
D. It requires all expenses to be allocated equally regardless of the period they relate to
questionBank.exp: The periodicity assumption requires the allocation of expenses between capital and revenue, since the economic life of the business is split into artificial periods.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the matching principle from the accrual principle?
opts: A. Matching sets revenue against the expenses that helped generate it; accrual records transactions when they occur, not when cash moves
B. Matching applies only to revenues; accrual applies only to expenses incurred during the year
C. Matching is a legal requirement; accrual is a voluntary practice adopted only by some firms
D. Matching and accrual are identical concepts with no meaningful distinction between them
questionBank.exp: The accrual principle provides the foundation for the matching principle: accrual recognizes transactions when they occur, while matching specifically sets expenses against the revenues they helped generate.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would be classified as a liability rather than an asset?
opts: A. A warehouse owned outright and used for storing inventory
B. A bank overdraft representing amounts owed to the bank
C. Computers used by staff for day-to-day administrative work
D. Cash held in hand for routine business transactions
questionBank.exp: A bank overdraft is a liability because it represents an amount owed to the bank, unlike the warehouse, computers, and cash, which are all assets.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of the term 'capital' in the accounting equation?
opts: A. The total amount of liabilities owed by a business to its external creditors
B. The residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities of the business
C. The total revenue earned by a business during a single accounting period
D. The amount of cash a business has invested in fixed assets to date
questionBank.exp: Capital is the residual interest in the assets of a business after deducting all of its liabilities, representing what would be left for the owner.

questionBank.q: In a limited liability company, which term is used in place of 'capital' to describe the owners' stake?
opts: A. Liability, since shareholders technically owe the company their initial investment
B. Revenue, since shareholders' returns are generated from company income
C. Equity, since this term describes the owners' residual interest in a limited company
D. Drawings, since shareholders may withdraw funds at their own discretion
questionBank.exp: In a limited liability company, the term 'equity' is used instead of 'capital' to describe the owners' residual interest in the business.

questionBank.q: Why does the rearranged equation 'Assets = Capital + Liabilities' more clearly reflect the format of the Statement of Financial Position?
opts: A. Because it lists liabilities before assets, matching how creditors are paid first
B. Because assets are presented first and balance with total equity and liabilities, just as on the statement
C. Because it eliminates the need to separate current and non-current items entirely
D. Because capital is always shown as a negative figure in this rearranged format
questionBank.exp: This format mirrors the Statement of Financial Position, where assets are presented first and the total balances with the combined figure for equity and liabilities.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why total debits always equal total credits in the accounting equation?
opts: A. Because assets are debits while capital and liabilities are both recorded as credits
B. Because liabilities are debits while capital and assets are both recorded as credits
C. Because capital is always recorded as a debit balance regardless of the transaction type
D. Because revenue and expense accounts are excluded entirely from the accounting equation
questionBank.exp: In the format Assets (Dr) = Capital (Cr) + Liabilities (Cr), assets are recorded as debits while capital and liabilities are recorded as credits, ensuring debits equal credits.

questionBank.q: How do drawings differ fundamentally from business expenses in their effect on the accounting equation?
opts: A. Drawings increase liabilities, while expenses always increase the value of assets
B. Drawings reduce capital directly, while expenses reduce capital through reducing profit
C. Drawings have no effect on capital, while expenses always increase total capital
D. Drawings and expenses have an identical effect on every account in the equation
questionBank.exp: Drawings reduce capital directly as withdrawals by the owner, while expenses reduce capital indirectly by reducing the profit that flows into capital.

questionBank.q: Why does the dual aspect of accounting guarantee that the accounting equation always remains balanced?
opts: A. Because every transaction results in equal and offsetting effects somewhere in the equation
B. Because every transaction is recorded twice in the same account for verification purposes
C. Because liabilities are adjusted manually at year-end to force the equation to balance
D. Because only transactions involving cash are recorded under the accounting equation
questionBank.exp: The dual aspect of accounting ensures that every transaction results in equal and offsetting increases or decreases somewhere within the equation, keeping it balanced.

questionBank.q: Which item in the expanded accounting equation directly reduces the owner's claim on the business's assets?
opts: A. Liabilities owed to external creditors and suppliers of the business
B. Income earned by the business from its trading activities during the period
C. Drawings taken by the owner for personal use during the period
D. Capital introduced by the owner at the start of the business
questionBank.exp: Drawings directly reduce the owner's claim on the business's assets, as amounts withdrawn by the owner decrease the capital balance.

questionBank.q: What happens to the accounting equation when a transaction affects only one side, such as an asset increasing while another asset of equal value decreases?
opts: A. The equation becomes temporarily unbalanced until the next adjusting entry is made
B. The equation remains balanced because total assets are unaffected by the internal swap
C. The equation requires an adjustment to liabilities to restore the balance afterward
D. The equation cannot reflect this type of transaction under standard accounting rules
questionBank.exp: When one asset increases while another decreases by an equal amount, total assets are unaffected, and the equation remains balanced without further adjustment.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would correctly be classified as an asset rather than a liability?
opts: A. A loan made by the business to another individual, to be repaid to the business
B. An amount owed by the business to a supplier for inventory purchased on credit
C. A sum the business owes to its bank in the form of an overdraft facility
D. An amount the business has been invoiced for but has not yet paid
questionBank.exp: A loan made by the business to another individual is an asset, since the business has the right to receive repayment, unlike the other items which are liabilities.

questionBank.q: Within the expanded accounting equation, where does income (revenue) fit conceptually?
opts: A. It is treated as a direct reduction to the liabilities side of the equation
B. It is treated as a component that increases capital through increasing profit
C. It is treated as a separate balance entirely disconnected from capital
D. It is treated identically to drawings as a reduction in owner's equity
questionBank.exp: Income increases capital by contributing to profit, which forms part of the owner's residual interest in the business.

questionBank.q: Why is it useful to think about just one account, such as cash, when analysing the effect of a transaction on the accounting equation?
opts: A. Because cash is the only account ever affected by a genuine business transaction
B. Because knowing the effect on one account lets you deduce the corresponding effect elsewhere
C. Because all other accounts automatically remain unaffected once cash has been considered
D. Because liabilities can never be affected by any transaction involving the cash account
questionBank.exp: If you know how a transaction affects one account, such as cash, you can use your knowledge of the accounting equation to deduce the corresponding effect on the other account.

questionBank.q: How would taking out a bank loan and depositing the proceeds in the business bank account affect the accounting equation?
opts: A. Assets increase and capital increases by an equal amount, leaving liabilities unaffected
B. Assets increase and liabilities increase by an equal amount, leaving capital unaffected
C. Liabilities increase and capital decreases by an equal amount, leaving assets unaffected
D. Assets decrease and liabilities increase by an equal amount, leaving capital unaffected
questionBank.exp: Taking out a bank loan increases cash (an asset) and creates a corresponding loan payable (a liability), leaving capital unaffected by the transaction itself.

questionBank.q: Why is the accounting equation considered foundational to the double-entry system of bookkeeping?
opts: A. Because it confirms that only cash transactions need to be recorded under double entry
B. Because it eliminates the need to separately record liabilities under double-entry rules
C. Because every double-entry transaction must keep the equation in balance through dual effects
D. Because the equation only applies to corporations and not to sole proprietorships
questionBank.exp: The accounting equation is the foundation for double-entry accounting because every transaction recorded under double entry must keep assets equal to liabilities plus equity.

questionBank.q: If a transaction increases an asset and simultaneously increases capital, what type of transaction is most likely involved?
opts: A. The repayment of a loan previously taken from a financial institution
B. The payment of an expense such as rent or electricity for the period
C. An additional cash investment made into the business by its owner
D. The purchase of inventory on credit from an established supplier
questionBank.exp: An additional cash investment by the owner increases an asset (cash) and increases capital simultaneously, unlike loan repayments, expense payments, or credit purchases.

questionBank.q: Why is double-entry bookkeeping often described using the phrase 'a coin has two sides'?
opts: A. Because every transaction must be recorded in two different currencies for accuracy
B. Because every transaction has two effects that must both be reflected in the books
C. Because every transaction must be approved by two separate signatories before posting
D. Because every transaction is recorded twice in the same account for verification
questionBank.exp: The phrase reflects the principle that every transaction has two sides or effects, both of which must be recorded to keep the books in balance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly completes the rule: an increase to a liability account is recorded as a ___, and a decrease to a liability account is recorded as a ___?
opts: A. Debit; Credit
B. Credit; Debit
C. Credit; Credit
D. Debit; Debit
questionBank.exp: Liabilities carry a normal credit balance, so increases are recorded as credits and decreases are recorded as debits.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly completes the rule: an increase to an expense account is recorded as a ___, and a decrease to an expense account is recorded as a ___?
opts: A. Credit; Debit
B. Debit; Credit
C. Debit; Debit
D. Credit; Credit
questionBank.exp: Expense accounts carry a normal debit balance, so increases are recorded as debits and decreases are recorded as credits.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly completes the rule: an increase to a revenue account is recorded as a ___, and a decrease to a revenue account is recorded as a ___?
opts: A. Debit; Credit
B. Credit; Debit
C. Debit; Debit
D. Credit; Credit
questionBank.exp: Revenue accounts carry a normal credit balance, so increases are recorded as credits and decreases are recorded as debits.

questionBank.q: Which step in the six-step transaction analysis process comes immediately before deciding on the debit and credit treatment?
opts: A. Identifying whether the transaction qualifies as an accounting transaction at all
B. Determining whether the affected accounts increase or decrease as a result
C. Determining the two accounts involved in the financial transaction itself
D. Determining the monetary amount involved in the transaction overall
questionBank.exp: The six-step process determines whether accounts increase or decrease immediately before the step of deciding whether each is debited or credited.

questionBank.q: Why are internal transactions, such as depreciation, sometimes more difficult to analyse than external transactions?
opts: A. Because internal transactions always involve a third party outside of the business
B. Because internal transactions may not have an accounting source document to evidence them
C. Because internal transactions are never recorded under any circumstances in the books
D. Because internal transactions require approval from external auditors before being recorded
questionBank.exp: Internal transactions involve only the business itself and may not have an accounting source document, making them harder to identify and analyse than external transactions.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a simple journal entry from a compound journal entry?
opts: A. A simple entry involves only cash transactions, while a compound entry involves only credit
B. A simple entry debits and credits one account each, while a compound entry involves three or more accounts
C. A simple entry is recorded in the ledger, while a compound entry is recorded only in the journal
D. A simple entry is reversible, while a compound entry can never be reversed once posted
questionBank.exp: A simple entry involves one debit and one credit account, while a compound entry involves three or more accounts connected to a single transaction.

questionBank.q: Which book of original entry would be used to record the correction of an error discovered in the ledger accounts?
opts: A. The Sales Journal, since corrections relate to revenue accounts exclusively
B. The Purchases Journal, since corrections typically relate to supplier balances
C. The Cash Book, since most correcting entries involve cash adjustments
D. The General Journal, since it is used for non-routine entries such as corrections
questionBank.exp: The General Journal is used for non-routine items, including the correction of errors found in the ledger accounts, as well as opening entries and asset disposals on credit.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes why posting reference numbers are useful between the journal and ledger?
opts: A. They allow an auditor to identify which employee approved a transaction
B. They allow users to trace an entry from the journal to its ledger posting and back
C. They are required only for transactions recorded in foreign currency
D. They eliminate the need to record a description for any journal entry
questionBank.exp: Posting reference numbers create a cross-reference, allowing users to trace an entry from the journal to its corresponding posting in the ledger, and vice versa.

questionBank.q: Under the double entry rule, which side of the accounting equation do liabilities, capital, and revenue normally fall on?
opts: A. The left side, the same side as assets and expenses
B. The right side, opposite to where assets and expenses fall
C. Neither side, since they are excluded from the accounting equation entirely
D. Both sides simultaneously, depending on the nature of the transaction
questionBank.exp: Liabilities, capital, and revenue fall on the right side of the accounting equation, opposite to assets and expenses, which fall on the left side.

questionBank.q: Once the rule for assets is mastered in double-entry bookkeeping, why can the rules for the remaining account types be derived from it?
opts: A. Because liabilities, capital, revenue, and expenses behave identically to assets in every case
B. Because the remaining account types simply mirror or oppose the asset rule depending on their position in the equation
C. Because only assets are ever debited, while every other account type is always credited
D. Because liabilities and capital are not subject to any debit or credit rules at all
questionBank.exp: The manual notes that once the asset rule is mastered, the rules for other account types can be derived, since they either mirror or oppose the asset treatment based on their position in the accounting equation.

questionBank.q: Which type of error involves an item being correctly classified as an asset, but posted to the wrong specific asset account?
opts: A. An error of principle, since the item type is fundamentally misclassified
B. An error of commission, since the amount is posted to the wrong account of the correct type
C. An error of omission, since the transaction was never recorded at all
D. A compensating error, since two unrelated errors offset one another
questionBank.exp: An error of commission occurs when an amount is correctly posted in terms of account type but to the wrong specific account, such as one asset account instead of another.

questionBank.q: Which type of error involves an item being recorded in a fundamentally wrong category of account, such as an expense being treated as an asset?
opts: A. An error of commission, since the wrong specific account was selected for posting
B. An error of principle, since the item is incorrectly classified by account type
C. A partial omission, since only one side of the entry has been recorded
D. A transposition error, since the figures were reversed during posting
questionBank.exp: An error of principle occurs when an item is incorrectly classified by account type, such as recording an expense as an asset, rather than simply posting to the wrong specific account.

questionBank.q: Why does a partial reversal of entry not necessarily cause the trial balance to be unequal?
opts: A. Because both sides of the transaction are still posted, just to the same side of each account
B. Because the transaction is excluded entirely from both the journal and the ledger
C. Because the amounts involved are always too small to affect the trial balance totals
D. Because a partial reversal only ever affects revenue and expense accounts, not assets
questionBank.exp: In a partial reversal, both sides of the transaction are posted, but to the same side of the respective accounts, which can still leave debits equal to credits despite the error.

questionBank.q: What is the defining feature that separates a 'book of original entry' from the general ledger in the accounting cycle?
opts: A. The book of original entry is prepared only once a year, unlike the general ledger
B. The book of original entry is where transactions are first documented before any further posting
C. The book of original entry contains only liability and equity accounts
D. The book of original entry replaces the need for any subsequent ledger posting
questionBank.exp: Books of original entry, such as journals, are where financial transactions are first documented before being posted to the general ledger.

questionBank.q: Which of the following transactions would most appropriately be recorded using a compound journal entry?
opts: A. A cash sale of goods to a single walk-in customer for an exact amount
B. A single payment by cheque covering both rent and electricity expenses together
C. A credit purchase of inventory from one supplier on standard credit terms
D. A cash withdrawal made by the owner for strictly personal use
questionBank.exp: A single payment covering two separate expense accounts, such as rent and electricity, requires a compound entry involving more than one debit account.

questionBank.q: In double-entry bookkeeping, what is the practical significance of always recording the debit entry before the credit entry?
opts: A. It is a strict legal requirement enforced by financial reporting regulators
B. It is simply a conventional sequence that helps maintain consistency and balance in recording
C. It changes which account is treated as the asset account in the transaction
D. It determines whether the transaction is treated as routine or non-routine
questionBank.exp: Recording the debit entry before the credit entry is a conventional sequence accountants follow to help ensure the accounting equation remains in balance, rather than a legal mandate.

questionBank.q: Why would the purchase of a non-current asset on credit be recorded in the General Journal rather than the Purchases Journal?
opts: A. Because the Purchases Journal is reserved specifically for credit purchases of goods for resale
B. Because non-current assets can never be purchased on credit under accounting rules
C. Because the General Journal is reserved exclusively for cash-based transactions
D. Because non-current asset purchases must always be recorded in the Sales Journal instead
questionBank.exp: The Purchases Journal is used specifically for credit purchases of goods for resale, so the credit purchase of a fixed asset is instead recorded in the General Journal.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why the trial balance would still balance even if a transaction were completely omitted from the books?
opts: A. Because both the debit and credit sides are simply missing together, leaving the totals equal
B. Because omitted transactions are automatically corrected by the suspense account
C. Because the trial balance only includes transactions involving cash receipts
D. Because the omission always affects only liability and equity accounts equally
questionBank.exp: If a transaction is completely omitted, neither the debit nor the credit side is recorded, so the trial balance totals remain equal despite the missing transaction.

questionBank.q: What is the key difference between an 'error of original entry' and a 'transposition error'?
opts: A. An error of original entry posts an incorrect amount to both accounts; a transposition error posts the wrong amount to only one side
B. An error of original entry affects only the credit side; a transposition error affects only the debit side
C. An error of original entry is never revealed by the trial balance, but a transposition error always is
D. An error of original entry and a transposition error are simply two names for the exact same mistake
questionBank.exp: An error of original entry posts the same incorrect amount to both the debit and credit sides, while a transposition error involves using one figure for the debit and a different (transposed) figure for the credit.

questionBank.q: Why is the trial balance described as a check on 'arithmetic accuracy' rather than a guarantee of overall correctness?
opts: A. Because it only confirms that debit and credit totals are numerically equal, not that postings are correct
B. Because it only applies to businesses that use manual, paper-based accounting systems
C. Because it is prepared before any journal entries have been recorded for the period
D. Because it automatically corrects any errors of principle found within the ledger
questionBank.exp: The trial balance confirms that total debits equal total credits, which checks arithmetic accuracy, but it cannot detect errors like omissions or misclassifications that leave the totals equal.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why source documents are considered the starting point of the accounting cycle?
opts: A. Because they are prepared by auditors after the financial statements are finalized
B. Because they provide the original evidence from which transactions are identified and analysed
C. Because they are only required for transactions exceeding a certain monetary threshold
D. Because they replace the need for journals and ledgers in modern accounting systems
questionBank.exp: Source documents provide the original evidence of a transaction, from which accountants identify and analyse transactions before recording them in the journal.

questionBank.q: What distinguishes the Sales Ledger from the General Ledger in a typical business's accounting system?
opts: A. The Sales Ledger contains personal accounts of credit customers, while the General Ledger contains real and nominal accounts
B. The Sales Ledger contains only cash transactions, while the General Ledger contains only credit transactions
C. The Sales Ledger is prepared annually, while the General Ledger is prepared on a daily basis
D. The Sales Ledger replaces the need to prepare a trial balance for the business
questionBank.exp: The Sales Ledger holds personal accounts for individual credit customers, while the General Ledger contains the real and nominal accounts, such as assets, expenses, and capital.

questionBank.q: Why might a business choose to use a Cash Book in addition to the General Ledger?
opts: A. Because the Cash Book replaces the need for a trial balance to be prepared at period end
B. Because the Cash Book provides a dedicated record of cash and cheque receipts and payments
C. Because the Cash Book is the only book legally required for tax reporting purposes
D. Because the Cash Book contains exclusively credit transactions with regular suppliers
questionBank.exp: The Cash Book provides a dedicated, specialized record for cash and cheque receipts and payments, separate from the broader General Ledger.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes a 'compensating error' in the context of trial balance preparation?
opts: A. An error where a transaction is recorded with unequal debit and credit amounts
B. An error where two or more separate mistakes happen to cancel each other out
C. An error where a transaction is recorded twice in the same ledger account
D. An error where a liability account is mistakenly treated as an asset account
questionBank.exp: A compensating error occurs when two or more separate errors happen to offset one another, meaning the trial balance can still balance despite the underlying mistakes.

questionBank.q: Why does an 'error of commission' fail to be revealed by the trial balance?
opts: A. Because the correct amount is still posted as a debit and credit, just to the wrong specific account of the same type
B. Because the transaction is omitted from the books entirely and never recorded
C. Because the wrong amount is used for both the debit and credit entries
D. Because the transaction always involves an asset account being treated as a liability
questionBank.exp: An error of commission still results in equal debits and credits being posted; the only mistake is posting to the wrong specific account of the same type, so the trial balance still balances.

questionBank.q: Which of the following items would typically be posted from the Cash Book rather than from the Sales or Purchases Journal?
opts: A. A credit sale of goods to a regular trade customer
B. A credit purchase of inventory from an established supplier
C. A cash payment made to settle an outstanding utility bill
D. The depreciation charge calculated for the accounting period
questionBank.exp: A cash payment for a utility bill is recorded in the Cash Book, since it involves an actual cash transaction, unlike credit sales, credit purchases, or depreciation adjustments.

questionBank.q: What is the primary reason a business prepares a trial balance before attempting to draw up its financial statements?
opts: A. To ensure ledger postings are arithmetically balanced before relying on them for reporting
B. To permanently close all temporary accounts before the new accounting period begins
C. To calculate the exact amount of tax owed for the current accounting period
D. To replace the need for preparing a Statement of Financial Position altogether
questionBank.exp: A trial balance is prepared to confirm that ledger postings are arithmetically balanced before using those balances to prepare the financial statements.

questionBank.q: Why would 'errors of principle' be considered more serious in nature than typical errors of commission?
opts: A. Because they distort the fundamental classification of accounts, not just the specific account used
B. Because they are the only type of error that the trial balance is able to detect
C. Because they only occur in businesses that do not use a double-entry system
D. Because they automatically result in unequal debit and credit totals every time
questionBank.exp: Errors of principle distort the fundamental classification of an item, such as recording an expense as an asset, which is a more significant misclassification than simply posting to the wrong account of the same type.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the General Journal and specialized journals like the Sales Journal?
opts: A. The General Journal handles non-routine transactions, while specialized journals handle high-volume, repetitive transaction types
B. The General Journal and specialized journals record identical transactions for cross-verification purposes
C. The General Journal is used only by corporations, while specialized journals are used only by sole proprietors
D. The General Journal replaces the need for any ledger postings related to specialized journal entries
questionBank.exp: The General Journal is reserved for non-routine transactions, while specialized journals like the Sales Journal handle high-volume, repetitive transactions of a similar type efficiently.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes why 'errors of omission' are considered among the hardest to detect during an audit?
opts: A. Because the transaction is missing entirely, leaving no trace of unequal debits and credits
B. Because they always involve unequal debit and credit totals in the trial balance
C. Because they only occur within the General Journal and never in specialized journals
D. Because they automatically trigger an entry in the suspense account for review
questionBank.exp: Since the transaction is missing entirely, there is no unequal debit or credit to draw attention to it, making errors of omission difficult to detect through the trial balance alone.

questionBank.q: Why is a credit balance in a Bank account on the trial balance interpreted differently from a credit balance in a typical asset account?
opts: A. Because a credit balance in the Bank account always reflects an arithmetic error
B. Because a credit Bank balance signals an overdraft, a liability, rather than a positive asset balance
C. Because Bank accounts are never permitted to carry a credit balance under any circumstances
D. Because a credit Bank balance is automatically transferred to the suspense account
questionBank.exp: A credit balance in the Bank account reflects an overdraft, which is a liability, rather than the normal debit balance expected of an asset like cash at bank.

questionBank.q: What is the main reason closing entries are necessary before a new accounting period begins?
opts: A. To permanently remove asset and liability accounts from the general ledger
B. To reset temporary accounts to zero so performance can be compared across periods
C. To eliminate the need to ever prepare another trial balance in the future
D. To convert all liability accounts into permanent equity accounts for reporting
questionBank.exp: Closing entries reset temporary accounts, such as revenue and expense accounts, to zero so that performance can be meaningfully compared from one period to the next.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best explains why the post-closing trial balance excludes revenue and expense accounts?
opts: A. Because revenue and expense accounts are permanent accounts carried forward indefinitely
B. Because revenue and expense accounts have already been closed and reduced to zero balances
C. Because revenue and expense accounts are not part of the double-entry system at all
D. Because revenue and expense accounts are recorded only in subsidiary ledgers, not the general ledger
questionBank.exp: By the time the post-closing trial balance is prepared, revenue and expense accounts have already been closed to zero through the closing entries, so they no longer appear.

questionBank.q: Why might a business prefer to record routine credit sales in a Sales Journal rather than the General Journal?
opts: A. Because the Sales Journal allows similar high-volume transactions to be grouped and processed efficiently
B. Because the General Journal cannot legally be used to record any form of revenue transaction
C. Because the Sales Journal eliminates the need to ever post entries to the general ledger
D. Because credit sales must always bypass the journal stage and go directly to the ledger
questionBank.exp: Specialized journals like the Sales Journal allow businesses to group and process high-volume, similar transactions efficiently, rather than recording each individually in the General Journal.

questionBank.q: What is the key distinction between a 'real account' and a 'nominal account' within the general ledger?
